items.originalTitle: We charge $10k a week to delete AI-generated code
items.summary:
Odra.dev offers a service designed to reduce AI-generated codebases by up to 65%, aiming to improve maintainability and functionality. The company provides a free initial analysis and, if beneficial, commits to a fixed-price contract with a clear reduction target. Their process includes a detailed review of the application, code consolidation, and rebuilding complex parts, supported by a two-week warranty to fix any issues introduced during the cleanup.

The service involves a week of focused work by three senior engineers for $10,000, with payment adjusted based on the percentage of the reduction target achieved. Odra.dev emphasizes maintaining code readability and functionality, using AI tools under strict expert supervision to ensure quality. They encourage direct communication and offer their expertise to teams struggling with bloated AI-generated codebases.

items.title: Bona Books reveals it accidentally accepted AI-generated stories in its 2025 queer speculative fiction anthology, prompting new editorial safeguards [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Honey, We Bought an AI Story
items.summary:
Bona Books disclosed that it inadvertently accepted AI-generated stories in its 2025 queer speculative fiction anthology, "Wrath Month," which featured 606 submissions from diverse queer writers. The discovery came after an editor noticed AI-like patterns in submissions from an author using the pseudonym Bella Chacha, prompting a thorough review that revealed multiple AI-generated entries had been included or considered for publication. Bona Books, a micro-press committed to promoting human authors, has since implemented new editorial safeguards to prevent similar incidents in the future.

The anthology, intended to channel LGBTQIA+ community anger into meaningful speculative fiction, faced significant challenges as the team worked to verify author identities and the authenticity of submissions. The situation highlighted the growing difficulty small presses encounter in distinguishing AI-generated content, especially as AI writing tools become more sophisticated. Bona Books' experience underscores broader concerns in the publishing industry about maintaining integrity and supporting genuine human creativity amid advancing AI technologies.

items.title: Developer uses Anthropic's Claude with Beagle SCM to automate coding tasks but finds LLMs remain imprecise and clumsy, advocating for deterministic tools and workflows to improve reliability [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Automating AI Away
items.summary:
A developer using Anthropic's Claude with Beagle SCM to automate coding tasks finds that while the language model is capable and insightful, it remains imprecise and prone to errors, such as mistakenly committing unwanted files. The developer highlights the inherent non-determinism and clumsiness of large language models (LLMs) compared to deterministic tools like parser generators, which produce formally correct code instantly.

To address these challenges, the developer advocates integrating LLMs with fast, deterministic tools and formal workflows that can guide, correct, and verify the model's outputs. Beagle SCM supports this approach by allowing LLMs to script routines in JavaScript layered over reliable C implementations, enabling automation of repetitive tasks and verification steps. This combination aims to harness the strengths of LLMs while mitigating their inconsistencies through structured, deterministic processes.

items.title: Rowboat launches open-source, local-first desktop AI coworker with built-in tools and knowledge graph for Mac, Windows, and Linux [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Rowboat – Open-source, local-first alternative to Claude Desktop
items.summary:
Rowboat is an open-source, local-first desktop AI coworker available for Mac, Windows, and Linux that organizes your work into a living knowledge graph to assist with tasks. It features integrated tools such as an email client, notes, browser, code mode, meeting note taker, and project workspaces, all designed to collaborate with AI while keeping data stored locally in plain Markdown.

Unlike many AI tools that reconstruct context on demand, Rowboat maintains long-term memory by accumulating context over time with explicit, editable relationships. It supports various AI models, including local and hosted options, and can connect to external tools and services through the Model Context Protocol, enabling integrations with platforms like web search, voice services, and project management tools.

Rowboat emphasizes user control and privacy by storing all data locally without proprietary formats or cloud lock-in, allowing users to inspect, edit, back up, or delete their information at any time. This approach aims to provide a more persistent and transparent AI assistant experience tailored to individual workflows.

items.title: zkSecurity's AI audit found and helped fix seven bugs in Cloudflare's CIRCL cryptography library, including critical float64 precision and access-control issues [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI Meets Cryptography 1: What AI Found in Cloudflare's Circl
items.summary:
zkSecurity's AI audit system, zkao, identified and helped fix seven vulnerabilities in Cloudflare's CIRCL cryptography library, including critical issues like float64 precision loss in threshold RSA and an access-control flaw in attribute-based encryption. These bugs were confirmed and addressed upstream, with several earning bounties through Cloudflare's HackerOne program. The audit combined AI-generated candidate findings with human validation to ensure accuracy and exploitability.

The process involved running large language models both independently and with expert-maintained skills to scan open source cryptography projects. zkao not only detected all previously found vulnerabilities but also uncovered more complex issues. This effort is part of an ongoing series exploring AI's capabilities in cryptographic code auditing and aims to refine automated security analysis by understanding AI reasoning patterns and improving validation efficiency.

items.title: Analysis: Anthropic's AI spending remains dominant despite rising open source model usage, reflecting a two-tier AI market lifecycle [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Why the rise of open source AI isn’t hurting Anthropic ... yet
items.summary:
Despite the growing use of open source AI models, spending on advanced models from frontier labs like Anthropic remains strong, indicating a two-tier market in AI development. Open source models tend to dominate mature, production-level applications, while frontier models lead in early-stage, high-cost deployments, maintaining their market share and premium pricing.

Data from platforms like Vercel and OpenRouter show that while open source models handle a larger volume of tokens, frontier models still account for the majority of AI spending due to their higher costs per token. This dynamic suggests that the rise of open source AI is complementing rather than displacing frontier labs, as the expanding AI market supports both phases of the technology lifecycle.

This two-tier structure may become a stable feature of the AI economy, with frontier labs focusing on discovery and innovation, and open source models managing established use cases. The continued dominance of premium frontier models highlights the complexity and diversity of AI applications, ensuring that both approaches coexist and thrive.

items.title: Security researcher earns $92,337 bug bounty for discovering GhostLock Linux kernel zero-day affecting major distributions since 2011
items.originalTitle: We won $92,337 bug bounty using a single kernel 0-day
items.summary:
A security researcher named VEGA discovered a critical Linux kernel vulnerability called GhostLock (CVE-2026-43499), which has affected all major Linux distributions since 2011. This zero-day flaw allows an unprivileged local attacker to escalate privileges and escape containers by exploiting a dangling pointer in the kernel's real-time mutex implementation. For this discovery and its exploitation, the researcher was awarded $92,337 through Google's kernelCTF bug bounty program.

GhostLock originated from a misuse of a kernel function that incorrectly handled task pointers during certain futex operations, leading to a stable privilege escalation path without requiring special kernel configurations or privileges. The vulnerability was introduced in Linux kernel version 2.6.39 and was fixed in version 7.1, meaning many systems remain vulnerable if not updated. The detailed technical analysis highlights the importance of patching and upgrading to the latest long-term support Linux versions to mitigate this long-standing security risk.

This surge significantly outpaces last year's $3.1 billion operating profit and exceeds recent growth reported by competitors like Micron Technology. items.originalSummary:
Samsung, it seems, deserves a little more respect. The electronics conglomerate may be best known in the U.S. for its TV sets and smartphones, which jostle with the iPhone for attention, but it’s also one of the three biggest makers of memory chips globally (along with Micron Technology and SK Hynix). The explosion of that business, thanks to demand from AI data centers, has turbocharged profits at all three companies—with Samsung providing fresh evidence of that on Tuesday.

Samsung issued a “pre-earnings guidance” notification—which we usually see from companies about to drop bad news they think investors need to hear as soon as possible—that its second-quarter operating profit would be about 89.4 trillion Korean won, or $59 billion. That would be up 1,800% on the year-earlier operating profit of just $3.1 billion. That’s even better than the 1,435% growth Micron reported in its operating profit a couple of weeks ago for the May quarter. Hynix, which is planning to list on the Nasdaq later this week, hasn’t yet reported for the second quarter. (Ironically, investors sold Samsung stock 7% down on Tuesday, apparently expecting even better growth—some people are never satisfied.)

items.title: The Information reports prolonged valuation write-downs in enterprise software startups amid rising adoption of cheaper AI alternatives [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Prolonged Write-Downs in Enterprise Software Startups
items.summary: Enterprise software startups are experiencing extended valuation write-downs as companies increasingly adopt more affordable AI alternatives. This trend is exemplified by an Atlanta real estate manager who replaced Salesforce with a custom app built using Replit and Claude Code, resulting in significant cost savings. The shift toward cheaper AI tools is impacting both public stock prices and private company valuations, with mutual fund disclosures revealing a generally pessimistic outlook among major investors.

items.originalSummary:
It’s not easy to run an enterprise software company these days. For the nth example of this, read the latest story by my colleague Laura Bratton, who describes how an Atlanta real estate manager replaced Salesforce software with a custom app developed using Replit and Claude Code—saving $100,000 a year. Yipes. 

Fears that companies will replace their software subscriptions with cheaper AI tools have hammered not just publicly traded stocks but the valuations of private companies. While we don’t often get a look at these private valuations unless the startups sell more shares, mutual fund disclosures give a glimpse into how big public investors are feeling. As the attached chart shows, for most it’s pretty bleak.

items.title: Qualcomm acquires Nexa AI and open-sources GenieX, a GenAI runtime for Snapdragon Hexagon NPUs supporting LLMs and VLMs [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Qualcomm acquires Nexa AI, open-sources GenAI runtime for Hexagon NPUs
items.summary:
Qualcomm has acquired Nexa AI and open-sourced GenieX, a GenAI inference runtime designed for Qualcomm Snapdragon devices. GenieX enables local execution of large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) on Snapdragon Hexagon NPUs, Adreno GPUs, or CPUs, supporting models from Hugging Face and Qualcomm AI Hub. The runtime offers multiple interfaces including CLI, Python, Android SDK, Docker, and an OpenAI-compatible server, facilitating easy integration and deployment on Qualcomm platforms.

GenieX supports a broad range of models with optimized performance on Snapdragon hardware, providing developers with tools to run frontier AI models locally. The project encourages community contributions and offers extensive documentation, sample apps, and support channels to assist users in leveraging the runtime for AI applications on Qualcomm devices.

items.title: European Commission proposes plan to manage risks and leverage opportunities of advanced AI in cybersecurity, including AI model evaluation and secure testing platforms [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: EU plan to address the risks and opportunities of advanced AI for cybersecurity
items.summary:
The European Commission has introduced a comprehensive plan to manage the risks and capitalize on the opportunities of advanced artificial intelligence in cybersecurity. The initiative aims to enhance the EU's cybersecurity by evaluating AI models, establishing secure testing platforms, and improving access to advanced AI systems for both public and private sectors.

The plan includes creating an EU evaluation capacity for AI risk assessment, developing a European blueprint for accessing advanced AI capabilities, and launching a secure platform for testing AI in cybersecurity contexts. It also emphasizes reinforcing cyber hygiene, risk management, and security by design principles to protect critical infrastructure, supported by guidance from the EU Agency for Cybersecurity. Additionally, the Commission plans to invest in European AI capabilities through initiatives like the EU Grand Challenge on AI for cybersecurity, fostering collaboration among companies, researchers, and organizations.

This strategy builds on existing EU regulations such as the AI Act and the Cyber Resilience Act, aiming to strengthen the EU's digital security framework and promote the safe and effective use of AI technologies in cybersecurity.

items.title: Researchers analyze probabilistic copying of training data by generative AI models and its implications for originality, privacy, and intellectual property [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Probabilistic "Copies" in Generative AI Models [pdf]
items.summary:
A recent study examines how generative AI models can produce probabilistic reproductions of their training data, sometimes generating exact or nearly identical segments. The research investigates the balance between creativity and memorization in these models and considers the implications for originality, data privacy, and intellectual property rights.

The paper analyzes the conditions under which generative AI systems replicate training data and explores the potential risks and challenges this poses for protecting sensitive information and respecting copyright. Understanding this phenomenon is crucial for developing guidelines and technologies that ensure responsible use of AI-generated content.

items.originalTitle: Meta just launched a new AI generator, Muse Image, and users are already pushing back over use of their photos
items.summary:
Meta has launched Muse Image, a new AI image generator accessible through the Meta AI app, Instagram Stories, and WhatsApp. The tool allows users to create images using public Instagram photos by tagging the original user, raising privacy concerns about consent and data use. Meta states users can control this feature through settings, but content created with AI will not trigger notifications to the original photo owners.

Muse offers various applications, including creating custom ads, experimenting with interior decorating ideas linked to Facebook Marketplace, and editing images with prompt-based commands. Meta is providing the service for free for everyday use, with subscription plans required beyond certain limits. The company is also developing Muse Video, an AI video generator, as part of its expanding AI offerings.

items.title: OpenAI uses a split WebRTC architecture with stateless relays and stateful transceivers to deliver low-latency voice AI to 900 million weekly users [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: How OpenAI Delivers Low-Latency Voice AI for 900M Users
items.summary:
OpenAI delivers low-latency voice AI to 900 million weekly users by employing a split WebRTC architecture that separates stateless relays from stateful transceivers. This design addresses the challenges of running WebRTC on Kubernetes, which treats server addresses as disposable, by using a stateless relay for geographic packet routing and a stateful transceiver to manage WebRTC connections and state. The system ensures quick connection setup and stable, low round-trip times to maintain natural, conversational voice AI interactions.

The architecture leverages the ICE ufrag field for routing, enabling efficient session handling across distributed infrastructure. OpenAI's approach builds on the Pion WebRTC library and incorporates optimizations such as Redis caching and socket-level enhancements. This setup supports continuous audio streaming, allowing the AI to process speech in real time, which is critical for a seamless user experience. The solution reflects deep expertise from OpenAI engineers, including contributors to WebRTC's original design.

items.originalTitle: Facing a Revolt, HubSpot Reverses Decision to Use Customer Data For AI Feature
items.summary:
HubSpot reversed its plan to use customer data from its CRM platform to power a new AI-driven sales lead feature after facing significant backlash from customers. The company had initially announced that it would collect and share certain customer data by default, requiring users to opt out if they did not want their information used. This decision sparked concerns about data privacy and led HubSpot to retract the plan within four days.

The incident highlights growing sensitivity among software users regarding data usage in AI applications and demonstrates the influence customers now hold over software providers. HubSpot's reversal also comes amid broader industry pressures, including fears that AI advancements could impact traditional software business models and customer retention.

items.originalSummary:
HubSpot last week triggered a firestorm among customers after announcing a plan to use some of the data they store with HubSpot’s customer relationship management app to power a forthcoming AI-powered feature.

While HubSpot reversed course four days later, the episode shows how sensitive customers are to software firms using their data in the AI era. HubSpot’s reversal is also another demonstration of the leverage that businesses have with the traditional software firms nowadays. We've noted before that some large customers have been able to shorten their contracts with software firms, which are keen not to lose clients given fears of rising competition from AI companies.

Let’s get back to HubSpot, whose shares are down 75% since early last year on fears AI would hurt its business and whose executives said sales growth would be slightly slower this year compared to last year.

On July 1, HubSpot announced it would use some customer data for a new AI feature that helps customers find new sales leads, which was set to launch next month.

HubSpot told customers in an email that it would collect such data by default and that customers would have to manually cut off access if they didn’t want Hubspot collecting it. HubSpot also said it may share their data, including “business contact details, employer information, and email deliverability signals,” with other customers. (HubSpot also said it had updated its terms of service, privacy policy and other customer agreements to reflect the change in its data collection practices.)

items.title: Goodfire researchers introduce Block-Sparse Featurizers to decompose vision model activations into multidimensional subspaces, revealing interpretable features and enabling fine-grained steering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural Geometry in Vision Models with Block-Sparse Featurizers
items.summary:
Goodfire researchers have developed Block-Sparse Featurizers (BSF), a new method to analyze vision model activations by decomposing them into multidimensional subspaces rather than single directions. This approach reveals interpretable, multidimensional features within the models, offering a more nuanced understanding of their internal representations and enabling precise control over model behavior. The findings suggest that most concepts in vision models are inherently multidimensional, challenging previous methods that treated concepts as one-dimensional.

BSFs provide a more accurate and parsimonious explanation of neural network activations by capturing the complex, curved structures that represent concepts in the models. This advancement improves interpretability and offers new tools for fine-grained manipulation of model outputs, marking a significant step forward in understanding and steering neural networks in computer vision applications.

It enables AI agents to query data, perform analyses using SQL, and generate shareable charts and reports without requiring a separate codebase or hosted database.

The platform normalizes diverse data sources into a unified schema, allowing consistent querying across multiple datasets including unemployment figures, trade flows, and monetary data. Users can install and authenticate the plugin easily, after which AI agents automatically invoke it to answer economic and financial questions with up-to-date information. FactIQ aims to enhance AI-driven economic analysis by integrating official statistics and live market insights into a single accessible tool.

items.title: Meta rolls out Muse Image AI model allowing anyone to generate images using public Instagram photos unless users opt out in settings [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Meta Now Lets Anyone Use Your Instagram Photos in AI Images—Unless You Opt Out
items.summary:
Meta has introduced its Muse Image AI model, which allows users to generate images using public Instagram photos by tagging the account in a prompt. By default, public Instagram profiles are automatically included in this feature, enabling others to create AI-generated images based on their content unless users actively opt out through the app's settings.

To prevent their photos from being used in AI-generated images without switching to a private account, Instagram users must adjust the new toggle found under the Sharing and reuse section in the app's settings. Meta does not notify users when their content is used in AI creations, and existing AI-generated images will remain even if users opt out later.

He played a significant role in upholding OpenAI's nonprofit mission and worked closely with senior leaders to advocate for government regulations that align with the goal of ensuring artificial general intelligence benefits all humanity.

Achiam's departure comes amid several leadership changes in OpenAI's safety and policy teams as the company evolves from a research lab into a major tech firm. He was known for his dedication to AI safety and made a notable appearance in the Musk v. Altman trial, highlighting his influence within the AI community. OpenAI has not yet announced a successor for his role, which bridged AI research and policy efforts.

items.originalTitle: Microsoft joins AI cost-cutting trend by relying more on its own models
items.summary:
Microsoft is reducing its reliance on AI models from OpenAI and Anthropic by deploying its own in-house AI models in popular applications like Excel and Word as part of a cost-saving strategy amid rising AI expenses. This shift reflects a broader industry trend where major tech companies are cutting back on AI spending to manage the high costs associated with third-party AI services.

The company has introduced several new proprietary models, including an agentic coder and a text-to-image generator, aiming to handle a growing share of user prompts internally. This move follows similar cost-cutting measures by other tech giants such as Amazon, Uber, Meta, and Accenture, highlighting the financial pressures within the AI sector and prompting some firms to explore alternative, more affordable AI solutions.

items.originalTitle: Meta’s new Muse Image model can pull other Instagram users into AI photos
items.summary:
Meta has introduced Muse Image, its first AI image generation model developed by the Superintelligence Labs division. This model now powers image creation tools across the Meta AI app, Instagram, and WhatsApp, with plans to expand to Facebook and Messenger. Muse Image allows users to include others in AI-generated photos by @ mentioning their Instagram accounts, using public photos to build visuals while giving users control over how their content is used.

The Muse Image model works alongside Meta's Muse Spark language model to interpret prompts, search the web, and plan image generation. It supports features like transforming images with suggested prompts, designing invitations and postcards, and redesigning rooms using images from Facebook Marketplace or other sources. Additionally, users can edit photos by drawing directly on them and share the results across Meta's platforms. The model will also power 30 new AI effects coming soon to Instagram Stories in the US before a wider rollout.

items.title: Discord admits AI moderation bug wrongfully banned over 8,000 users since May for harmless images including spreadsheets and game textures, now restoring affected accounts [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Discord admits AI moderation bug wrongfully banned users over harmless images
items.summary:
Discord has acknowledged a bug in its AI moderation system that wrongfully banned over 8,000 users since May for uploading harmless images such as spreadsheets, chessboards, and game textures. The issue led to automatic bans without proper human review, but the company has since fixed the problem and is restoring affected accounts. This incident underscores the challenges of relying on automated systems for content moderation, which can produce false positives despite safeguards.

The bug caused the AI to misidentify certain benign images as harmful content, triggering immediate account suspensions. Discord explained that its system matches uploaded content against databases of known harmful material, but a flaw bypassed the usual human review step. Users affected by the bans expressed frustration, highlighting the impact on those who depend on Discord for work and community engagement.

This event reflects broader concerns about AI moderation errors on social platforms, with similar issues reported by Instagram, Facebook, and Tumblr. Discord has committed to improving safeguards to prevent such wrongful bans in the future, aiming to balance effective moderation with minimizing harm to legitimate users.

items.title: EU AI Act becomes applicable August 2, 2026, imposing auditable obligations on high-risk AI systems with penalties up to €35M or 7% of global turnover [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: EU AI Act becomes applicable Aug 2: an engineering checklist
items.summary:
The EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) will become applicable on August 2, 2026, imposing legally binding obligations on high-risk AI systems used in areas such as hiring, credit scoring, education, and critical infrastructure. These obligations require continuous risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, human oversight, and proof of system accuracy and security. Non-compliance can result in penalties up to €35 million or 7% of global annual turnover, similar to GDPR fines.

The regulation emphasizes treating compliance as an integral part of the AI system's design and operation, rather than a post-hoc documentation exercise. It mandates versioned classification of AI systems, ongoing risk registers, automated bias testing, and audit-ready logging. Providers must also ensure clear instructions for users, effective human oversight features, and rigorous evaluation of system robustness and security with evidence maintained throughout the software development lifecycle.

This approach aims to embed conformity into engineering practices, aligning compliance with continuous integration and deployment pipelines. Organizations are encouraged to adopt these practices proactively to meet the EU AI Act's requirements and avoid significant financial penalties, marking a shift towards treating regulatory compliance as a core engineering discipline.

items.title: sqlite-utils 4.0 released with database schema migrations, nested transactions, and compound foreign key support [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: sqlite-utils 4.0, now with database schema migrations
items.summary:
sqlite-utils 4.0 has been released, introducing major new features including database schema migrations, nested transactions via a new db.atomic() method, and support for compound foreign keys. This release marks the first major version update since 3.0 in 2020 and includes some breaking changes detailed in the upgrade guide. The migration system allows defining and applying schema changes programmatically in Python, tracking applied migrations, and supports enhanced table transformations beyond SQLite's native capabilities.

The migration feature builds on a design originally released as a separate package called sqlite-migrate, now integrated into sqlite-utils to benefit the broader ecosystem. Nested transactions leverage SQLite savepoints for safer and more manageable database operations. Additionally, the release improves upsert behavior, query execution methods, and data import type detection. The development process involved extensive testing and refinement aided by AI tools, resulting in a higher-quality and more robust release.

items.originalSummary:
This morning I released sqlite-utils 4.0, the 124th release of that project and the first major version bump since 3.0 in November 2020. In addition to some small but significant breaking changes (described in this upgrade guide), this version introduces three major features: database migrations, nested transactions (via a new db.atomic() method), and support for compound foreign keys.

Database schema migrations using sqlite-utils

Schema migrations define a sequence of changes to be made to a SQLite database, plus a mechanism for tracking which migrations have been applied and applying any that are found to be pending.

Migrations are defined in Python files using the sqlite-utils Python library, which includes a powerful table.transform() method providing enhanced alter table capabilities that are not supported by SQLite's ALTER TABLE statement.

(table.transform() implements the pattern recommended by the SQLite documentation - create a new temporary table with the new schema, copy across the data, then drop the old table and rename the temporary one in its place.)

Here's an example migration file which creates a table called creatures, adds an additional column to it in a second step, then changes the types of two of the columns in a third:

from sqlite_utils import Migrations migrations = Migrations("creatures") @migrations() def create_table(db): db["creatures"].create( {"id": int, "name": str, "species": str}, pk="id", ) @migrations() def add_weight(db): db["creatures"].add_column("weight", float) @migrations() def change_column_types(db): db["creatures"].transform(types={"species": int, "weight": str})

Save that as migrations.py and run it against a fresh database like this:

uvx sqlite-utils migrate data.db migrations.py

Then if you check the schema of that database:

uvx sqlite-utils schema data.db

You'll see this SQL:

CREATE TABLE "_sqlite_migrations" ( "id" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, "migration_set" TEXT, "name" TEXT, "applied_at" TEXT ); CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "idx__sqlite_migrations_migration_set_name" ON "_sqlite_migrations" ("migration_set", "name"); CREATE TABLE "creatures" ( "id" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, "name" TEXT, "species" INTEGER, "weight" TEXT );

The _sqlite_migrations table is used to keep track of which migration functions have been run. The creatures table above is the schema after all three migrations have been applied.

To see a list of migrations, both pending and applied, run this:

uvx sqlite-utils migrate data.db migrations.py --list

Output:

Migrations for: creatures Applied: create_table - 2026-07-07 17:58:41.360051+00:00 add_weight - 2026-07-07 17:58:41.360608+00:00 change_column_types - 2026-07-07 18:01:15.802000+00:00 Pending: (none)

If you don't specify a migrations file, the sqlite-utils migrate data.db command will scan the current directory and its subdirectories for files called migrations.py and apply any Migrations() instances it finds in them.

You can also execute migrations from Python code using the migrations.apply(db) method, which is useful for building tools that manage their own database schemas over multiple versions. My own LLM tool has been using a version of this pattern for several years now, as shown in llm/embeddings_migrations.py.

Prior art

My favorite implementation of this pattern remains Django's Migrations, developed by Andrew Godwin based on his earlier project South. Fun fact: Andrew, Russ Keith-Magee, and I presented our competing approaches to schema migrations for Django on the Schema Evolution panel at the very first DjangoCon back in 2008! My attempt was called dmigrations, developed with a team at Global Radio in London.

Django's migrations can be automatically generated from model definitions and include the ability to roll back to a previous version. The sqlite-utils approach is deliberately simpler: unlike Django, sqlite-utils encourages programmatic table creation rather than a model definition ORM, so there isn't anything we can use to automatically generate migrations.

I decided to skip rollback, since in my experience it's a feature that is rarely used. With a SQLite project, an easy way to achieve rollback is to create a copy of your database file before you apply the migrations!

Migrating from sqlite-migrate

The design of sqlite-utils migrations is three years old now - I had originally released it as a separate package called sqlite-migrate, which never quite graduated beyond a beta release.

I've used that package in enough places now that I'm confident in the design, so I've decided to promote it to a feature of sqlite-utils to make it available by default to all of the other tools in the growing sqlite-utils/Datasette/LLM ecosystem.

I made one last release of sqlite-migrate, which switches it to depend on sqlite-utils>=4 and replaces the __init__.py file with the following:

from sqlite_utils import Migrations __all__ = ["Migrations"]

Any existing project that depends on sqlite-migrate should continue to work without alterations.

Everything else in sqlite-utils 4.0

Here are the release notes for this version, with some inline annotations:

The 4.0 release includes some minor backwards-incompatible fixes (hence the major version number bump) and introduces three major new features:

  • Database migrations, providing a structured mechanism for evolving a project’s schema over time. (#752)

I think of migrations as the signature new feature, hence this blog post.

  • Nested transaction support via db.atomic(), plus numerous improvements to how transactions work across the library. (#755)

sqlite-utils has long had a confused relationship with database transactions, partly because when I started designing the library back in 2018 I didn't yet have a great feel for how those worked in SQLite itself.

Adding migrations to the core library made me determined to finally crack this nut, since transactions make migration systems a whole lot safer and easier to reason about.

I ended up building this around a db.atomic() context manager which looks like this:

with db.atomic(): db.table("dogs").insert({"id": 1, "name": "Cleo"}, pk="id") db.table("dogs").insert({"id": 2, "name": "Pancakes"})

SQLite supports Savepoints, and as a result db.atomic() can be nested to carry out transactions inside of transactions. It's pretty neat!

  • Support for compound foreign keys, including creation, transformation and introspection through table.foreign_keys. (#594)

This came about when I asked a coding agent to review all open issues and PRs for things that should be included in a 4.0 release since they would represent breaking changes if I added them later, and it correctly identified that compound foreign keys were exactly that kind of feature.

I started with a breaking change to the table.foreign_keys introspection method, and then decided to see if Claude Fable 5 could handle the more fiddly job of integrating compound foreign key creation into the library. The API design it helped create felt exactly right to me - consistent with how the rest of the library worked already.

Other notable changes include:

  • Upserts now use SQLite’s INSERT ... ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE SET syntax, detect existing table primary keys automatically and reject records that are missing required primary key values. (#652)

This was the change that first pushed me to consider a breaking-change 4.0 version bump. I built this to help support sqlite-chronicle, which uses triggers to keep track of rows in a table that have been inserted, updated or deleted.

  • db.query() now executes immediately and rejects statements that do not return rows; use db.execute() for writes and DDL.

Probably the most disruptive breaking change - I've had to update a few places in my own code to switch from db.query() to db.execute() as a result.

  • CSV and TSV imports now detect column types by default, while inserts into existing tables preserve those tables’ column types. (#679)

The sqlite-utils insert data.db creatures creatures.csv --detect-types flag was a later addition to allow column types (text, integer, real) to be automatically detected based on the data in a CSV. It should be the default, and releasing a 4.0 means I can make it so.

  • table.extract() and extracts= no longer create lookup table records for all-null values. (#186)

The oldest issue addressed by this release - the underlying bug was opened (by me) in October 2020.

See Upgrading from 3.x to 4.0 for details on backwards-incompatible changes.

The detailed release notes for the features and fixes shipped during the 4.0 pre-release cycle are available in 4.0a0, 4.0a1, 4.0rc1, 4.0rc2, 4.0rc3 and 4.0rc4.

The upgrade guide was entirely written by Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5. The same is true of the release notes.

This is the kind of documentation I've slowly become comfortable outsourcing to the robots. It doesn't need to convince people of anything, or express any opinions - its job is to be as accurate and detailed as possible. I've reviewed the release notes closely and can confirm they are accurate and comprehensive.

Claude Fable 5 helped a lot

I released the first alpha of sqlite-utils 4.0 over a year ago. I've been dragging my heels on the stable release because of the amount of work it would take to track down and clean up the many other minor design flaws that a major version number allowed me to take on.

Assistance from Claude Fable 5 (and to a lesser extent Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5) gave me just the boost I needed to overcome inertia and make the most of the time I could afford to spend on this library.

Fable has really good taste in API design, and is relentlessly proactive if you give it a more open goal. My most successful prompt was a review task that I issued against what I thought was the last release candidate:

review the changes on main since the last tagged 3.x release - I am about to ship them as sqlite-utils 4.0, a stable version that promises no backwards-incompatible fixes for a very long time.

review the changelog and upgrade guide, and write yourself scratch scripts to try out all of the new features in v4 - save those scripts but don't commit them

I tried this with GPT-5.5 xhigh in Codex Desktop and Fable 5 in Claude Code.

GPT-5.5 wrote 5 Python scripts and didn't turn up anything particularly interesting - its final report is here.

Fable 5 wrote 12 scripts, identified 4 release blockers and 10 additional issues in its report, and built a neat combined repro script, which, when run, output the following:

=== 1. Failed db.execute() write leaves an implicit transaction open === in_transaction after failed write: True BUG: table 'other' silently lost when connection closed === 2. Leading ';' bypasses the query() first-token scanner === BUG: raised OperationalError: no such savepoint: sqlite_utils_query BUG: row persisted despite rollback (count=1) === 3. Rejected write PRAGMA via query() still takes effect === BUG: user_version=5 after 'rejected' statement (docs say no effect) === 4. Implicit compound FK resolves pk columns in table order, not PK order === BUG: other_columns reported as ('b', 'a'), should be ('a', 'b') BUG: transform of valid data raised IntegrityError: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed === 5. ForeignKey (now a dataclass) is no longer hashable === BUG: cannot use 'sqlite_utils.db.ForeignKey' as a set element (unhashable type: 'ForeignKey') === 6. Mixed ForeignKey objects and tuples in foreign_keys= rejected === BUG: foreign_keys= should be a list of tuples === 7. insert --csv into an EXISTING table transforms its column types === BUG: existing zip '01234' is now 1234 (column type: int) === 8. insert(pk=, alter=True) regression: InvalidColumns before alter runs === BUG: InvalidColumns: Invalid primary key column ['id'] for table t with columns ['a'] === 9. migrate --stop-before an already-applied migration applies everything === BUG: m2 was applied despite --stop-before m1 (m1 already applied) === 10. ensure_autocommit_on() silently commits an open transaction === BUG: row survived rollback (count=1) - transaction was committed

I found myself agreeing with almost all of them. Here's the PR with 16 commits where we worked through them in turn.

There's no doubt in my mind that sqlite-utils 4.0 is a significantly higher-quality release than if I had built it without the assistance of the latest frontier models.

items.title: Momentic migrates caching system from PostgreSQL to ClickHouse to handle over 2 million daily queries and 20 billion entries with 250 ms average latency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Switching from PostgreSQL to ClickHouse for Improved Performance and Scalability
items.summary:
Momentic, an AI-driven software testing platform, has rearchitected its caching system by migrating from PostgreSQL to the column-oriented database ClickHouse to manage over 2 million daily queries and 20 billion entries while maintaining an average response latency of around 250 milliseconds. This transition addressed performance issues caused by rapid cache growth and high read-write workloads that PostgreSQL struggled to handle efficiently.

The migration involved running ClickHouse alongside PostgreSQL initially, duplicating writes to both systems and gradually shifting traffic after validating results. Momentic optimized query performance by designing an effective primary key and using materialized views to reduce data scanning. Additionally, they simplified query patterns and eliminated the Redis caching layer by leveraging ClickHouse's asynchronous deduplication features, resulting in improved scalability and reduced resource usage.

items.title: Researchers propose KARMA, a knowledge graph-based method for automated reasoning and slot-aligned contrastive candidate synthesis, outperforming baseline models across biomedical, computer science, and chemistry benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: KARMA: Knowledge graph-based Automated Reasoning Materialization and Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced KARMA, a novel method that leverages knowledge graphs for automated reasoning and slot-aligned contrastive candidate synthesis. KARMA addresses the Resolution Mismatch Problem by enumerating schema-constrained paths over domain knowledge graphs and converting them into slot-aligned contrastive candidates, improving the precision of preference supervision in model training.

The approach incorporates Slot-Parallel Alignment (SPA), which applies a decoupled slot-level objective to focus supervision on discriminative entity slots, supported by slot-aware masked attention for efficient evaluation. KARMA demonstrated superior performance compared to baseline large language models and same-data supervised fine-tuning methods across benchmarks in biomedical, computer science, and chemistry domains, and showed competitive results against sequence and token-level preference techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03166v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Template-based contrastive synthesis is scalable, but its candidates often differ only in a few entity-slots while sequence-level optimization spreads supervision over mostly shared templates. We formalize this as the Resolution Mismatch Problem and propose KARMA, which enumerates schema-constrained paths over domain knowledge graphs and verbalizes them into slot-aligned contrastive candidates. Slot-Parallel Alignment (SPA) then applies a decoupled slot-level objective to route preference supervision to discriminative entity-slots, with slot-aware masked attention serving as an optional packed-evaluation implementation. Across biomedical, computer-science, and chemistry benchmarks, KARMA outperforms base LLM and same-data SFT baselines, and compares favorably with sequence and token-level preference methods.

items.title: Researchers propose DMVM, a decentralized framework for efficient multi-task dataset valuation via model merging without retraining or data sharing, validated on vision and NLP tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Efficient Decentralized Multi-task Dataset Valuation via Model Merging
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced DMVM, a decentralized framework designed to efficiently evaluate datasets used in training multi-task models without the need for retraining or data sharing. This approach leverages model merging and task arithmetic to infer each dataset's contribution by analyzing how models trained on different datasets combine in parameter space. DMVM addresses limitations of existing methods that are typically single-task focused, computationally intensive, and unsuitable for decentralized environments with privacy constraints.

The framework includes a secure aggregation protocol that allows collaborative valuation without exposing individual model parameters or private data. Theoretical error bounds support the method's reliability, and extensive experiments on computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate its scalability, computational efficiency, and alignment with multi-task generalization behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Accurate and efficient dataset valuation is essential for enabling fair and transparent data marketplaces, especially when multiple contributors provide data for training multi-task models. Most existing valuation methods, however, are limited to single-task settings, overlooking scenarios where a buyer aims to optimize performance across multiple downstream tasks. Moreover, traditional valuation approaches, such as Shapley-based or retraining-based methods, are computationally expensive and poorly suited for decentralized environments without a trusted central coordinator and with strict privacy constraints. We propose DMVM (Decentralized Multi-task Valuation via Model Merging), a novel framework that bypasses retraining and data sharing by leveraging task arithmetic to infer dataset contributions directly from model combinations. Instead of retraining or sharing raw data, DMVM quantifies how models trained on different datasets combine in parameter space to infer each dataset's marginal utility across multiple tasks. This formulation yields a valuation process that is scalable, computationally efficient, and explicitly aligned with multi-task generalization behavior. To support decentralized deployment, we introduce a secure aggregation protocol that enables collaborative valuation without revealing individual model parameters or private data. We also provide theoretical error bounds characterizing the approximation quality of DMVM and validate our framework through comprehensive experiments on computer vision and natural language processing tasks.

items.title: CaresAI predicts independent TNM cancer staging using classical and deep learning models on TCGA pathology reports for SMM4H-HeaRD 2026 shared task [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CaresAI at SMM4H-HeaRD 2026: Predicting TNM Staging
items.summary:
This study presents CaresAI's approach to independently predicting Tumor, Node, and Metastasis (TNM) cancer staging using pathology reports from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) as part of the SMM4H-HeaRD 2026 shared task. The researchers framed the problem as three multi-label classification tasks and applied both classical and deep learning methods, including TF-IDF features and embeddings from ClinicalBERT, BioBERT, and PubMedBERT, combined with models such as Logistic Regression, LightGBM, Feed-Forward Neural Networks, and Wide Residual Networks. Their results showed that combining embeddings improved prediction accuracy, with LightGBM using TF-IDF achieving the highest AUROC and F1-scores during training.

Evaluation on test sets revealed strong Macro-F1 scores across TNM categories, though performance declined between test sets, indicating challenges with model generalizability, class imbalance, and processing lengthy clinical documents. While the study offers an efficient baseline model and reproducible pipeline, it highlights the need for further optimization and validation before clinical application.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03466v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study aims to predict Tumor, Node, and Metastasis (TNM) stage labels independently, with the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pathology report as the sixth shared task of SMM4H-HeaRD 2026. The problem is framed as three multi-label classification tasks. We explore both classical and deep learning approaches using Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) features and embeddings from ClinicalBERT, BioBERT, and PubMedBERT. These representations are used with Logistic Regression (LR), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), Feed-Forward Neural Networks (FFNN), and Wide Residual Networks (WRN). Our results show that individual embeddings perform similarly to the TNM label classification, while their combination improves its predictive ability. WRN achieves AUROC scores of 0.839 (T), 0.8502 (N), and 0.803 (M) with F1-scores of 0.622, 0.702, and 0.9337, respectively, for the training phase. LightGBM with TF-IDF performs best with AUROC scores of 0.9368 (T), 0.9524 (N), and 0.8311 (M) and F1-scores of 0.7559 (T), 0.7384 (N), and 0.7017 (M) during the training phase. Furthermore, the result of the Codabench for the test sets indicates a Macro-F1 score of 0.978, 0.957, and 0.879 for the T, N, and M categories respectively for test set 1; while test set 2 records a Macro-F1 score for T, N, and M is 0.807, 0.767, 1.0 respectively. However, performance declined during the evaluation phase of the test sets, a drop from 0.938 to 0.858 of test set 1 to 2, for the Macro-F1 score across all stages; suggesting limitations in model generalizability, sensitivity to class imbalance, and challenges in processing lengthy clinical documents. Although this study provides an efficient baseline model and a reproducible pipeline, further optimization and validation are required before it can be considered suitable for use in a real-world clinical setting.

items.title: Researchers decode hidden multi-step reasoning in frontier LLMs over filler tokens using unsupervised pipeline with 80-95% accuracy across four task families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reading Between the Dots: Decoding Hidden Computation across Filler Tokens
items.summary: Researchers have developed an unsupervised decoding pipeline that reveals how advanced large language models (LLMs) perform multi-step reasoning over content-free filler tokens, such as dots or counting sequences, with 80-95% accuracy across four task families including fact retrieval and string manipulation. This approach uncovers hidden computations within two open-weight models, DeepSeek V3 and Kimi K2, showing that these models process filler tokens in a structured manner despite the absence of visible chain-of-thought in their outputs. The findings suggest that the models' internal computational traces, rather than just their surface tokens, hold the key to understanding and monitoring their reasoning processes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier LLMs can perform multi-step reasoning over content-free filler tokens like dots or counting sequences, producing correct answers with no visible chain-of-thought (CoT). This is a limit case for behavioral oversight, where surface tokens carry no information about the underlying reasoning. But hidden from the output is not the same as hidden from us. On four task families (fact retrieval, parallel numeric composition, string manipulation, and in-context computation), two open-weights frontier models (DeepSeek V3, Kimi K2) compute over filler tokens in a structured, legible way: attention routes the question through the filler region to the answer, logit-lens readouts show retrieved facts emerging early and their composition crystallizing in late layers, and KV-cache transplants at filler positions causally swap outputs between examples. We introduce an unsupervised decoding pipeline that takes only hidden states as input and recovers intermediate values with 80-95% accuracy (best LLM judge) across both models and all four tasks, without ground-truth labels or training. Hidden computation that defeats behavioral CoT monitoring is, on these tasks, directly readable from the residual stream, suggesting monitorability is a property of the model's full computational trace, not just its surface tokens.

items.title: Researchers find language models represent communicative intent reliably across six models but often fail to act on it by default, with intent decodable before output generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: They Infer What You Meant: Models Represent Communicative Intent More Reliably Than They Act On It
items.summary:
Researchers have found that large language models reliably represent the communicative intent behind user inputs across six different models, but often fail to act on this intent by default. By analyzing hidden states within these models, the study shows that intent can be decoded well before it influences the model's output, indicating a gap between representation and behavior. This finding was consistent across multiple model families and types of intent, including both explicit and pragmatically inferred meanings.

The study used a linear probe to decode whether a user wanted their input recognized or evaluated, revealing that while the models internally represent this intent clearly, only some models act on it without additional prompting. The researchers identified a specific direction in the model's internal layers that, when manipulated, can steer the model to behave according to the intended communicative goal without explicit instructions. This suggests that the failure to act on intent is not due to lack of understanding but rather how the models read out and use this information.

These insights highlight a potential pathway to improve language model responsiveness by targeting the internal representations of intent, which could lead to more accurate and context-aware interactions. The findings also emphasize that the ability to represent intent does not guarantee appropriate action, pointing to important considerations for future model design and interpretability research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03598v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a person shares something with a language model, the model often answers the surface of the message rather than what the sender was doing by sending it: share a finished project and it critiques the code; share a raw late-night line and it runs a wellness check. We treat the sender's communicative intent, the Gricean what-was-meant, as a first-class interpretability object, and show the failure is one of readout on top of a robust representation. A linear probe decodes the sender's intent, whether they want a thing recognized or evaluated, from a model's default-pass hidden states, cleanly and surface-independently, across six models and four families and in the base checkpoints. The representation generalizes further, to intent that is only pragmatically inferred, and to a second, lexically clean intent (support versus help). The behavioral half of the story, and every causal test, is established on the recognize/evaluate contrast, where what varies is whether the default output acts on the intent. The readout lags the representation in depth within a model (the intent is decodable several layers before it drives the output); across models, which ones act on it by default is model-specific, an observed stratification (three of six show the failure) that we do not read as a scaling law. Where the gap is open, a direction closely tied to the representation, the discriminative direction at a searched-for layer, is a causal handle: steering it recovers the intended behavior, as well as an explicit instruction does and with no prompt at all. This direction is near-orthogonal to the feedback-offering axis, so it routes a represented intent rather than a generic feedback knob, though at the recovery dose the routed intent can override an explicit request. We support each link with controls against obvious deflations and report the nulls as plainly as the confirmations.

outputCleanup.description:
Researchers have found that large language models reliably represent the communicative intent behind user inputs across six different models, but often fail to act on this intent by default. By analyzing hidden states within these models, the study shows that intent can be decoded well before it influences the model's output, indicating a gap between representation and behavior. This finding was consistent across multiple model families and types of intent, including both explicit and pragmatically inferred meanings.

The study used a linear probe to decode whether a user wanted their input recognized or evaluated, revealing that while the models internally represent this intent clearly, only some models act on it without additional prompting. The researchers identified a specific direction in the model's internal layers that, when manipulated, can steer the model to behave according to the intended communicative goal without explicit instructions. This suggests that the failure to act on intent is not due to lack of understanding but rather how the models read out and use this information.

These insights highlight a potential pathway to improve language model responsiveness by targeting the internal representations of intent, which could lead to more accurate and context-aware interactions. The findings also emphasize that the ability to represent intent does not guarantee appropriate action, pointing to important considerations for future model design and interpretability research.

items.title: Researchers introduce Stabilized Adapter for self-Report (SAR) to detect hidden behaviors in fine-tuned language models, outperforming existing introspection methods across seven implanted behaviors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Revealing Hidden Model Behaviors with Task-Specific Self-Reports
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Stabilized Adapter for self-Report (SAR), a lightweight LoRA adapter designed to help fine-tuned language models reveal their hidden behaviors in plain language. SAR effectively detects subtle or harmful behaviors implanted during fine-tuning, outperforming existing introspection methods across seven tested behaviors and a control case. Unlike previous approaches, SAR maintains accuracy even when models exhibit broad misalignment beyond the training data's scope and significantly reduces hallucinations in behavior reporting.

SAR's ability to reliably identify hidden model behaviors makes it a valuable tool for practitioners seeking to audit and understand what their models have actually learned. This advancement addresses limitations in current introspection adapters, which sometimes fail to detect certain behaviors or produce incorrect reports, thereby improving transparency and trust in fine-tuned language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03640v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning can give a language model a hidden behavior--it may give false answers under a narrow condition, or give harmful advice only when a prompt touches a particular topic. We introduce the Stabilized Adapter for self-Report (SAR), a lightweight LoRA adapter that makes a fine-tuned model describe its own hidden behavior in plain language, using only the model and the dataset it was trained on. Across seven implanted behaviors (plus a no-behavior control), SAR detects the hidden behavior in every one--even when the model has generalized into broad misalignment that the training data alone does not predict. Introspection Adapters (IA), the closest existing baseline, detects some behaviors from our suite but misses others entirely--and where it misses, it hallucinates, consistently reporting wrong behaviors. SAR retains positive signal on every setting where IA fails and halves the rate of hallucinations. This makes it much easier for practitioners to audit their models and obtain reliable answers to "what did my model actually learn?" type of questions.

items.title: Researchers develop a local hidden-state probe to replace GPT-3.5 prompting for metadata filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG, achieving 90.9% accuracy on 2556 multi-hop queries with a 135M-parameter model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Probe, Don't Prompt: A Hidden-State Probe for Metadata Filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a local, deterministic hidden-state probe to replace GPT-3.5 prompting for metadata filtering in Multi-Meta-RAG, a system designed to improve retrieval in multi-hop question answering. This probe, trained on the hidden states of a small open-source language model, achieves 90.9% accuracy on 2,556 MultiHop-RAG queries, outperforming both a model-free substring baseline and GPT-3.5 prompting, particularly on queries where GPT-3.5 does not abstain. The probe's fixed output vocabulary prevents drift outside the allowed metadata sources, enhancing reliability.

The approach relies on three key design choices: selecting a shallow model layer, applying mean pooling, and using class-imbalance-aware multi-label training to handle a long tail of sources. A 135-million-parameter model performs nearly as well as a larger 1.5-billion-parameter model, making the filter computationally efficient by requiring only a partial forward pass through the initial layers and a linear classification head, without the need for API calls. The code for this method is publicly available on GitHub.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03929v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-Meta-RAG improves retrieval for multi-hop question answering by filtering a vector store on metadata (the news source) that it extracts from each query by prompting gpt-3.5-turbo. We show this proprietary, free-form extractor can be replaced by a local, deterministic probe trained on the hidden states of a small open-source language model. On all 2556 MultiHop-RAG queries the probe reaches 90.9% set-exact accuracy against 88.0% for a model-free substring baseline and 80.9% for GPT-3.5, a margin that comes entirely from null queries, on which GPT-3.5 never abstains; on non-null queries all three stay within about a point. Because the probe's output space is exactly the fixed 49-source vocabulary, it cannot drift outside the allow-list as the prompted model does. Three design choices make it work: selecting a shallow layer, mean pooling, and class-imbalance-aware multi-label training over the long tail of sources. A 135M-parameter model lands within ~1.5 points of a 1.5B one, so the filter is cheap to output: a partial forward pass through the first few layers plus one linear head, with no API. The code is available at https://github.com/mxpoliakov/Multi-Meta-RAG.

items.title: Researchers introduce Telescope Perplexity metric to improve zero-shot detection of LLM-generated text by measuring token repetition probability, showing state-of-the-art performance across datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Telescope: Improving Zero Shot Detection of LLM Generated Content By Measuring Token Repetition Probability
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new metric called Telescope Perplexity to improve the zero-shot detection of text generated by Large Language Models (LLMs). This metric measures the probability of token repetition, leveraging a bias in LLMs that strongly avoid repeating tokens early in their training. This characteristic, described as a "Vestigial Heuristic," helps distinguish LLM-generated text from human writing.

The study shows that the Telescope Perplexity signature appears early in the pre-training phase of LLMs and enables effective detection without additional training data. The method achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results across various datasets, reference models, and perturbation schemes, offering greater efficiency compared to existing detection techniques.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distinguishing Large Language Model (LLM) generated text from human writing is a critical and difficult challenge. While LLMs are trained to write like humans, we hypothesize that this training leaves an indelible mark. LLMs develop a particularly strong aversion to token repetition very early in training. This bias persists as a ''Vestigial Heuristic'' (a developmental artifact) that is activated in LLM-generated text, separating LLM from human writing. To probe this phenomenon, we introduce Telescope Perplexity, a metric that evaluates the token repetition of the model, $P(s_i | s_{1:i})$ . Our empirical investigation reveals that the Telescope Perplexity signature emerges early in pre-training, and Telescope Perplexity empirically enables highly effective zero-shot LLM detection. We show state-of-the-art or competitive performance across diverse datasets (including modern evaluation sets we introduce), reference models, and perturbation schemes with greater efficiency than other methods.

items.title: Researchers release MTEB-PT, a Portuguese sentence encoder benchmark evaluating 17 models across 14 datasets, showing task-dependent performance and benefits of language-specific fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Multilingual Averages: MTEB-PT, a Benchmark for Portuguese Sentence Encoders
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MTEB-PT, a new benchmark designed to evaluate Portuguese sentence embedding models across 14 datasets covering tasks such as semantic textual similarity, classification, retrieval, and reranking. The study assessed 17 open- and closed-source models, revealing that performance in Portuguese varies significantly by task and that multilingual model rankings do not consistently predict effectiveness for Portuguese-specific tasks. Models with enhanced long-context capabilities performed better on tasks involving longer inputs.

The benchmark also demonstrated that fine-tuning models specifically for Portuguese improves their performance, particularly when the fine-tuning data closely matches the target task. To explore this, the researchers fine-tuned three backbone models using Portuguese contrastive supervision and Matryoshka Representation Learning, achieving notable gains in semantic textual similarity and retrieval tasks. The team has made the MTEB-PT benchmark, fine-tuned models, and associated training and evaluation code publicly available to support further research in Portuguese language processing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04071v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Portuguese remains underrepresented in text embedding evaluation, despite being one of the most widely spoken languages in the world. As a result, embedding models are often selected based on English or multilingual metrics, while their effectiveness in Portuguese remains unclear. We present MTEB-PT, a Portuguese benchmark constructed from a subset of MMTEB, comprising 14 existing datasets across Semantic Textual Similarity (STS), classification, retrieval, and reranking. We use this benchmark to evaluate 17 open- and closed-source embedding models under a unified protocol. Our results show that Portuguese performance is strongly task-dependent: multilingual rankings do not reliably predict Portuguese-specific performance across task families, no single model dominates all settings, and models with stronger long-context capacity are particularly advantageous on longer-input tasks such as retrieval and reranking. The benchmark also shows that language-specific fine-tuning still improves model performance in Portuguese, especially on task types that match the adaptation data most closely. To examine this effect, we fine-tune three representative backbone models with Portuguese contrastive supervision and Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL). These benchmark-informed baselines yield their strongest gains on STS, consistent with the predominantly symmetric supervision used during training, while also improving retrieval and remaining competitive under dimensional truncation. We release the MTEB-PT benchmark, the fine-tuned models, and the training and evaluation code.

items.title: Researchers introduce GASP, a span-level detector for hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation, achieving improved accuracy on RAGTruth and TofuEval benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting Hallucinations in Retrieval-Augmented Generation through Grounding-Aware Sensitivity by Perturbation (GASP)
items.summary:
Researchers have developed GASP (Grounding-Aware Sensitivity by Perturbation), a new span-level detector designed to identify hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. Unlike existing detectors that provide only an overall answer-level score, GASP evaluates each sentence by measuring how its likelihood depends on the retrieved evidence, allowing it to pinpoint unsupported content. The method involves rescoring answers under varying contexts and analyzing changes in likelihood and divergence metrics to distinguish grounded sentences from hallucinated ones.

GASP was tested on three benchmarks—RAGTruth, TofuEval, and RAGBench—using multiple instruction-tuned models. It achieved significant improvements over traditional baselines such as perplexity and natural language inference, particularly on the RAGTruth dataset, where it reached a response-level AUC of about 0.73 and a span-level AUC of about 0.67. The approach is training-free and does not require labeled data, making it practical for detecting hallucinations in outputs closely tied to retrieved context rather than those relying on parametric knowledge.

The results suggest that GASP is especially effective for outputs constructed from retrieved information, with its performance transferring well to some benchmarks but not to short-answer question answering tasks. This highlights its potential for improving the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation systems by providing more granular and interpretable hallucination detection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04223v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces but does not eliminate hallucination, and existing detectors return a single answer-level score that does not indicate which sentence is unsupported, or why. To close this gap, we introduce Grounding-Aware Sensitivity by Perturbation (GASP), a span-level detector that scores each answer sentence by how strongly its likelihood depends on the retrieved evidence, a quantity we term grounding sensitivity. GASP holds the answer fixed and re-scores it under the full context, under no context, and with each chunk removed, then measures the log-likelihood drops and Jensen-Shannon divergences (JSD). The likelihood of a grounded sentence collapses once its supporting passage is removed, whereas a hallucinated sentence is almost unaffected, a contrast we interpret by casting decoding as a random nonlinear iterated function system (RNIFS). We evaluate GASP on three benchmarks (RAGTruth, TofuEval, RAGBench) with three instruction-tuned scorers from two model families (Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-1.5B, and SmolLM2-1.7B) under a leakage-clean protocol. On RAGTruth it reaches a response-level area under the ROC curve (AUC) of about 0.73 and a span-level AUC of about 0.67, improving significantly over perplexity and by clear margins over length, whole-context natural language inference (NLI), and self-consistency baselines. The only baseline competitive at the span level is a well-configured chunk-level entailment verifier, which requires a separate model, whereas a training-free threshold on the grounding features matches the trained classifier without labeled data and serves as the default detector. Beyond RAGTruth, the signal transfers to TofuEval but not to short-answer question answering in RAGBench, showing GASP is best suited to outputs constructed from the retrieved context rather than answers recoverable from parametric knowledge.

Researchers have developed GASP (Grounding-Aware Sensitivity by Perturbation), a new span-level detector designed to identify hallucinations in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. Unlike existing detectors that provide only an overall answer-level score, GASP evaluates each sentence by measuring how its likelihood depends on the retrieved evidence, allowing it to pinpoint unsupported content. The method involves rescoring answers under varying contexts and analyzing changes in likelihood and divergence metrics to distinguish grounded sentences from hallucinated ones.

GASP was tested on three benchmarks—RAGTruth, TofuEval, and RAGBench—using multiple instruction-tuned models. It achieved significant improvements over traditional baselines such as perplexity and natural language inference, particularly on the RAGTruth dataset, where it reached a response-level AUC of about 0.73 and a span-level AUC of about 0.67. The approach is training-free and does not require labeled data, making it practical for detecting hallucinations in outputs closely tied to retrieved context rather than those relying on parametric knowledge.

The results suggest that GASP is especially effective for outputs constructed from retrieved information, with its performance transferring well to some benchmarks but not to short-answer question answering tasks. This highlights its potential for improving the reliability of retrieval-augmented generation systems by providing more granular and interpretable hallucination detection.

items.title: Researchers present CausalGame benchmark to evaluate causal thinking of 30 LLM agents in 14 scientific discovery scenarios with selection bias and hidden confounders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: CausalGame: Benchmarking Causal Thinking of LLM Agents in Games
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CausalGame, a new benchmark designed to evaluate the causal reasoning abilities of large language model (LLM) agents in scientific discovery tasks. The benchmark challenges 30 LLM agents across 14 scenarios that simulate real-world issues such as selection bias, measurement error, and hidden confounders. Agents are required to design experiments, gather data, and provide explanations, testing their ability to distinguish causation from correlation and recognize hidden biases.

The study found that none of the tested LLM agents demonstrated reliable causal thinking, with the best model achieving only 68% effectiveness compared to analytical optima of 78-85%. Additionally, only 5-7% of sessions met the criteria for causal reasoning. CausalGame offers a scalable and controlled environment to assess and improve the causal inference capabilities of AI Scientist agents, addressing gaps in existing benchmarks that do not fully capture these complex challenges.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04293v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Building AI Scientist agents with Large Language Models (LLMs) has recently attracted growing attention. Since scientific discovery fundamentally relies on uncovering causal relationships from observations, the capability of causal thinking, i.e., distinguishing causation from correlation and recognizing hidden biases, is essential to LLM agents. Although a number of benchmarks exist for AI Scientists, none explicitly incorporate challenges from selection bias, measurement error, and hidden confounders that widely exist in real-world scientific discovery. To this end, we present CausalGame, a benchmark that evaluates the causal thinking capabilities of LLM agents through interactive games. CausalGame asks LLM agents to actively design experimental protocols, collect observation data, and derive a final solution with an explanation report. To emulate realistic scientific discovery challenges, we design 14 scenarios that incorporate selection bias, measurement error, and hidden confounders. Across 30 LLM agents, none demonstrates reliable causal thinking: the best model reaches only 68.0% survival against analytical optima of 78-85%, and merely 5-7% of sessions receive credits on the causal-reasoning rubrics. CausalGame provides a scalable and controlled testbed for evaluating the causal thinking of AI Scientist agents.
