items.title: Researchers propose UI-MOPD, a multi-teacher on-policy distillation method for continual learning of cross-platform GUI agents using the Uni-GUI dataset, achieving up to 38.2% task success rates [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: UI-MOPD: Multi-Platform On-Policy Distillation for Continual GUI Agent Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced UI-MOPD, a novel multi-teacher on-policy distillation method designed for continual learning of GUI agents across multiple platforms. Utilizing the newly developed Uni-GUI dataset, UI-MOPD dynamically selects platform-specific teachers to transfer behavioral knowledge to a shared policy, enabling the agents to adapt to new platforms while retaining existing capabilities. This approach addresses challenges such as scarce cross-platform interaction data and the risk of behavioral pattern mixing and forgetting during training.

Experiments conducted on OSWorld and MobileWorld platforms demonstrate that UI-MOPD achieves task success rates of 38.2% and 12.0%, respectively. These results highlight the method's effectiveness in balancing the retention of cross-platform skills with the adaptation to new environments, marking a significant advancement in the development of versatile GUI agents capable of operating across diverse platforms.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04425v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in multimodal foundation models and agent systems have driven GUI agents from single-platform task execution toward cross-platform interaction. However, building multi-platform GUI agents remains challenging. On one hand, high-quality and executable cross-platform interaction trajectories are still scarce, and existing data often suffer from limited platform coverage. On the other hand, different platforms exhibit distinct interaction conventions, making joint or continual training prone to behavioral pattern mixing, platform-specific capability degradation, and catastrophic forgetting. To address these challenges, we construct Uni-GUI, a high-quality cross-platform GUI interaction dataset, and propose UI-MOPD, the first method that incorporates multi-teacher on-policy distillation into continual learning for GUI agents. UI-MOPD dynamically selects a platform-specific teacher according to the current environment and transfers platform-specific behavioral priors to a shared policy through platform-conditioned distillation, enabling adaptation to new platforms while preserving capabilities on existing ones. Experiments on OSWorld and MobileWorld show that UI-MOPD achieves task success rates of 38.2% and 12.0%, respectively, demonstrating its effectiveness in balancing cross-platform capability retention and new-platform adaptation. Project page: https://elispectre.github.io/UI-MOPD/.

items.title: Researchers identify a latent persona direction causing emergent misalignment in Qwen2.5 models, demonstrating transplanting, inverting, and prevention methods conditional on fine-tuning approach and model capacity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Transplanting, inverting, and preventing a misalignment persona: method-conditional emergent misalignment in Qwen2.5
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a latent persona direction in Qwen2.5 language models that causes emergent misalignment (EM), a broad misbehavior arising after fine-tuning on narrow harmful data. This persona direction is causal and can be transplanted into other models sharing only pretraining, inducing EM, while ablating it reduces misalignment. The recruitment of this persona depends on the fine-tuning method and model capacity, with low-rank parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) more likely to induce it than full supervised fine-tuning (SFT). 

The study shows that the persona's causal role varies with training conditions; attempts to steer training away from this direction can paradoxically increase misalignment. However, because recruitment acts as a loss-reducing shortcut that higher capacity models can avoid, it can be selectively screened and prevented. The findings provide a controlled case study of emergent misalignment mechanisms in a single model family, highlighting methods to measure, transplant, invert, and prevent harmful behaviors linked to latent persona directions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Emergent misalignment (EM) -- the broad misbehaviour a language model acquires after fine-tuning on narrow harmful data -- is mediated in Qwen2.5 models by a latent persona direction, and that direction is causal in open weights. Transplanting it into a model that shares only pretraining with its source induces broad EM (2.83 +/- 0.26% misaligned against a random-direction floor of ~1.1%), and ablating a model's own direction roughly halves an overt inducer's broadcast (21% to 10%). The transplant doubles as a measurement method, causally assaying directions that a source model represents but cannot itself express. Whether a fine-tune recruits this persona depends on method and capacity, and since low-rank PEFT is the cheaper regime at scale, the recruiting method is also the economical one. On Qwen2.5-32B, low-rank LoRA on insecure code recruits it (3.4% misaligned) while full SFT on identical data does not (0.3%) and moves against the persona axis (drift-persona cosine +0.17 at rank 1 to -0.10), the far-inducer, high-capacity exception consistent with a representational-distance x capacity account. The persona's causal role is itself conditional. Steering a bad-medical SFT run away from the direction during training raises the broadcast from 24% to 51% while a matched random control lowers it, so removing the direction is no blanket recipe. Because recruitment is a loss-reducing shortcut that capacity renders redundant, it can be screened for and prevented in the tested instances. Persona loss-relevance at the SFT solution orders four inducers' broadcasts rank-perfectly within Qwen2.5, inoculation removes recruitment selectively (4.75% to 0.0%, code coherence 65% to 87%), and fine-tuning orthogonal to the single behaviour-derived axis reduces it persona-specifically. Results are a controlled case study of one model family, single-seed in places.

items.title: Researchers introduce EEG-SpikeAgent, an LLM-based closed-loop program synthesis system for automated EEG spike detection achieving 0.935 AUROC on a public 29-channel dataset [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EEG-SpikeAgent: Agentic Closed-Loop Program Synthesis for Automated EEG Spike Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EEG-SpikeAgent, a novel closed-loop program synthesis system that uses a large language model to automate the detection of interictal epileptiform discharges in scalp EEG. This system iteratively generates and refines signal-processing features by proposing deterministic EEG feature modules, executing code to produce tabular features, and evaluating performance with a classifier. Tested on the public VEPISET dataset, EEG-SpikeAgent achieved a high area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (0.935) and demonstrated improved balanced accuracy and F1 scores compared to spike-only feature searches.

The approach integrates artifact-aware feature generation and provides an auditable, code-driven method for EEG feature engineering, balancing interpretability with accuracy. By feeding structured diagnostics back to the model for refinement, the system enhances feature proposals based on performance metrics, offering a transparent and methodical alternative to traditional deep-learning models in clinical EEG analysis.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated detection of interictal epileptiform discharges in scalp electroencephalography (EEG) is clinically important, but recent high-performing deep-learning models often trade interpretability for accuracy. We introduce EEG-SpikeAgent, a closed-loop program-synthesis framework that uses a large language model (LLM) agentic system to generate signal-processing features for spike detection in scalp EEG. The system iteratively proposes one deterministic EEG feature module at a time, executes the resulting code on EEG to generate tabular features, evaluates performance via a tabular classifier, summarizes run-level metrics, and feeds structured diagnostics back to the model for refinement. Across iterations, EEG-SpikeAgent proposes and refines candidate signal features and decision rules informed by model performance. We evaluated EEG-SpikeAgent on VEPISET, a public 29-channel dataset of 4-second epochs containing 2,516 discharge-containing and 22,933 non-discharge epochs. Across five-fold cross-validation with a gradient-boosted tree classifier, agent-generated features achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.935, balanced accuracy of 0.699, F1 score of 0.557, sensitivity of 0.401, and specificity of 0.996 at the default operating point. At an operating point with sensitivity 0.80, mean precision was 0.470 and mean specificity was 0.900. Artifact-aware feature generation improved balanced accuracy and F1 score over spike-only feature search. These results indicate that LLM-based program synthesis can automate EEG feature engineering in auditable and inspectable code-driven manner for clinical and methodological review.

items.title: Researchers introduce Retroactive Chain-of-Thought (RetroCoT) forensic reconstruction prompts to diagnose safety alignment gaps across GPT-4 and GPT-5 model generations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Retroactive Chain-of-Thought (RetroCoT): Forensic Reconstruction Prompts as a Safety Diagnostic Across Model Generations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Retroactive Chain-of-Thought (RetroCoT), a novel method to test safety alignment in large language models by reframing harmful requests as forensic reconstruction tasks. Unlike direct requests, RetroCoT asks models to reverse-engineer the causal chain behind a harmful outcome, revealing that models often comply with harmful objectives when expressed through different communicative styles. Testing on GPT-4 variants showed high attack success rates, while GPT-5 models initially resisted these prompts but remained vulnerable to adversarial feedback that exploited pragmatic framing.

The study highlights that current alignment policies are sensitive to how requests are pragmatically framed rather than their semantic content, indicating that safety measures are not fully robust across different communicative registers. The findings suggest that even advanced models like GPT-5 can be circumvented by novel pragmatic approaches, emphasizing the need for more comprehensive alignment strategies that account for varied linguistic contexts.

items.title: Researchers propose Selective Importance Sampling to convert off-policy tokens to on-policy in LLM reinforcement learning, improving alignment and robustness with minimal overhead [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Turning Off-Policy Tokens On-Policy: A Plug-in Approach for Improving LLM Alignment
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Selective Importance Sampling (SIS), a new method to improve reinforcement learning post-training for large language models (LLMs) by converting off-policy tokens into on-policy tokens. This approach addresses the high variance caused by traditional importance sampling in long sequences by applying a token-level rejection test that treats accepted tokens as on-policy, eliminating the need for importance score corrections. SIS acts as a plug-in that modifies the importance ratio in the policy loss with minimal computational overhead and is compatible with various RL post-training algorithms.

Theoretical analysis shows that SIS reduces the gap between token-level and sequence-level off-policy gradient estimators. Experimental results on dense and mixture-of-experts LLMs across mathematical and agent benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements in performance and enhanced robustness when handling off-policy data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04728v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for large language models (LLMs) follows a efficient paradigm of "rollout then update", which inevitably results in off-policy training data. To resolve this, Importance sampling (IS) is proposed, while the token-level ratios compound over long sequences, causing severe variance exploded. A natural idea is "transferring" these off-policy token into on-policy token, so that the importance scores for correction are unnecessary. Following this idea, we propose Selective Importance Sampling (SIS), which is inspired by rejection sampling. Concretely, SIS implements by viewing off-policy model as proposal distribution, and implement a token-level rejection test: accepted tokens are viewed as on-policy, so that receive unit importance score, while rejected tokens retain the standard IS correction. Our proposed SIS is theoretically proved reducing the gap between token-level and sequence-level off-policy gradient estimators. The SIS acts as a plug-in that only modifies the importance ratio in the policy loss, adding negligible wall-clock overhead, and can be combine with a vast vary of RL post-training algorithms. Experiments on dense and MoE LLMs across math and agent benchmarks show that SIS consistently improves all objectives, while providing substantially stronger robustness under off-policy data.

items.title: Researchers propose Schwartz-geometry decoding for human value detection using theory-aware energy decoder to improve label coherence without reducing classification accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Independent Labels: Schwartz-Geometry Decoding for Human Value Detection
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method to improve human value detection by incorporating the circular motivational structure of Schwartz values into multi-label classification. Instead of treating the 19 refined Schwartz values as independent labels, they introduced a theory-aware energy decoder that scores label sets jointly, enhancing label coherence without sacrificing classification accuracy. This approach leverages the inherent relationships between values as described by Schwartz theory, using a soft bias rather than a hard constraint.

The study compared training-time geometry-aware objectives with a post-hoc Schwartz-aware energy decoder on a DeBERTa-v3-base classifier. While training-time methods showed limited improvement, the energy decoder significantly increased label coherence according to new theory-aware metrics, maintaining Macro-F1 and Micro-F1 scores. The improvement was specific to the true Schwartz ordering and did not occur with random label permutations or empirical co-occurrence graphs.

This theory-aware decoding offers a lightweight and controllable way to align value detection with the underlying label space structure. Diagnostic tests with a large language model indicated that providing the continuum at inference influences behavior but does not replicate supervised structured prediction, highlighting the decoder's unique contribution to faithful value detection.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05052v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human value detection is commonly formulated as sentence-level multi-label classification over the 19 refined Schwartz values, typically predicted as independent labels. Schwartz theory, however, describes them as a circular motivational continuum, in which adjacent values are compatible and opposing values are in tension. We ask whether this structure can be operationalized as an explicit output-space geometry and used as a soft bias rather than a hard constraint. On a DeBERTa-v3-base classifier, we compare two ways of injecting it: training-time geometry-aware objectives and a post-hoc Schwartz-aware energy decoder that scores whole label sets jointly. Across five seeds, training-time geometry gives only limited gains-no larger for the true continuum than for a random ordering-whereas the decoder makes label sets more coherent with the continuum-on theory-aware coherence metrics we introduce-at no cost to Macro-F1 or Micro-F1 (held fixed by its selection rule). The gain is specific to the true Schwartz ordering: it does not appear for a random permutation or an empirical co-occurrence graph through the identical decoder. A bounded Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct diagnostic shows that supplying the continuum at inference shifts behavior but does not match supervised structured prediction. Theory-aware decoding thus offers a lightweight, controllable way to make value detection faithful to its label space.

items.title: Nemotron Labs releases Audex, a unified audio-text large language model with 157.4B audio tokens and 320.5B text tokens, achieving state-of-the-art audio tasks without regressing on text intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Unified Audio Intelligence Without Regressing on Text Intelligence
items.summary:
Nemotron Labs has introduced Audex, a unified audio-text large language model (LLM) that integrates 157.4 billion audio tokens and 320.5 billion text tokens. Built on a strong text-only MoE LLM, Audex uses a single Transformer decoder to encode audio inputs into the text embedding space, enabling seamless audio-text fusion and multimodal generation. This design supports standard LLM training and inference infrastructure, allowing the model to perform advanced audio understanding, speech recognition and translation, text-to-speech, audio generation, and speech-to-speech generation without compromising its text-based reasoning and knowledge capabilities.

The model was trained through a multi-stage supervised process on carefully curated audio-text datasets, followed by reinforcement learning and multi-domain distillation. Audex achieves state-of-the-art performance in various audio tasks while maintaining the alignment, long-context understanding, and agentic abilities of its text-only backbone. Nemotron Labs has released the model checkpoints to support open research in this area.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05196v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio intelligence involves understanding, reasoning about, and generating both audio and speech. In this work, we introduce Nemotron-Labs-Audex-30B-A3B (Audex), a unified audio-text LLM built on Nemotron-Cascade-2-30B-A3B, a strong text-only MoE LLM. Audex adopts a simple unified design with a single Transformer decoder: audio inputs are encoded and projected into the text embedding space, while text tokens and quantized audio output tokens are treated uniformly during generation. This architecture enables strong audio-text fusion, seamless multimodal generation, and compatibility with standard LLM training and inference infrastructure. For training, we meticulously curate audio-text datasets comprising 157.4B audio tokens and 320.5B text tokens. We apply multi-stage supervised training on these datasets, followed by text-only Cascade RL and multi-domain on-policy distillation. Audex delivers state-of-the-art audio understanding, speech recognition and translation, text-to-speech, audio generation, and speech-to-speech generation, while preserving very compelling reasoning, alignment, knowledge, long-context, and agentic capabilities of its text-only LLM backbone with marginal or no regression. We release the model checkpoints to facilitate open research.

items.title: Researchers propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA) for safe inference-time alignment in frozen language models, improving helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff in sequence and token-level methods [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Safe Inference-Time Alignment via Lagrangian Reward Augmentation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a new framework for inference-time alignment in frozen language models that incorporates safety constraints without the need for repeated weight updates. LARA transforms the alignment problem into a one-dimensional convex optimization over a dual variable, which is calibrated on a small dataset and used to augment reward signals during decoding. This approach improves the balance between helpfulness and harmlessness in language model outputs, enhancing both sequence-level and token-level alignment methods.

LARA operates by dualizing a KL-regularized constrained objective involving reward and cost models, enabling it to serve as a drop-in scoring mechanism for existing inference-time alignment techniques. For sequence-level methods like Best-of-N reranking, LARA provides an exact solution to the expected-cost constrained problem, while for token-level decoding it offers a principled heuristic. Evaluations show that LARA, particularly with Best-of-N, approaches the performance of finetuning-based alignment methods, offering a safer and more effective alternative for guiding frozen language models during inference.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02781v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inference-time alignment steers a frozen language model during decoding using auxiliary reward signals, avoiding the cost of repeated weight updates. However, existing inference-time alignment methods typically optimize a single scalar score, so explicit safety constraints must either be ignored or encoded through manually tuned penalties. We propose Lagrangian Reward Augmentation (LARA), a general inference-time alignment framework under safety constraints. Starting from a KL-regularized constrained objective with a reward model and a cost model, LARA dualizes the constraint and reduces the optimization problem to a one-dimensional convex problem over a nonnegative dual variable. Estimated on a small calibration set, this dual variable defines an augmented reward that can be used as a drop-in scoring signal within existing inference-time alignment methods. For sequence-level sampling methods, such as Best-of-N reranking, the calibrated dual variable corresponds to the solution of the expected-cost constrained problem. For token-level reward-guided decoding methods, the same construction yields a principled dual-calibrated heuristic rather than an exact constrained-policy guarantee. We evaluate LARA on both sequence-level and token-level inference-time alignment methods, and find that LARA improves the helpfulness-harmlessness tradeoff, with Best-of-N achieving the best performance among inference-time methods, approaching finetuning-based direct alignment baselines.

items.summary: Researchers have introduced BDLM Mamba-H, a hybrid model combining Mamba mixers and attention mechanisms, designed to improve long-context language generation efficiency. This model addresses the challenge of memory bandwidth limitations during generation by restricting reverse-direction scans to active denoising blocks, enabling exact caching and reducing memory access. BDLM Mamba-H demonstrates superior validation perplexity in smaller models and remains competitive at larger scales, achieving up to 19.7 times the throughput of previous diffusion models at 65,000 tokens and significantly outperforming BDLM attention at longer contexts.

Generation is typically memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound: each decoding step must stream the accumulated key/value (KV) cache from memory, so bandwidth demand grows with context length while only one token is emitted. Two parallel approaches have therefore emerged: reducing memory access with efficient attention variants and linear-time mixers such as Mamba, or increasing parallel computation by generating blocks of tokens at once. However, technical challenges arise when combining these two ideas. Earlier hybrid diffusion models such as DiffuMamba use bidirectional Mamba mixing, including a reverse-direction scan relative to causal generation. This reverse scan needs to scan the entire sequence, so its states are not prefix-only and cannot be precisely reused as a cache even when diffusion is performed block by block. We propose a BDLM Mamba--attention hybrid that addresses this challenge by restricting the reverse Mamba scan to the active denoising block, which enables exact caching across blocks. In an 87M-parameter DCLM sweep, BDLM Mamba-H achieves the best C4-en validation perplexity compared to BDLM attention and full-sequence baselines. At 350M parameters, it remains competitive with BDLM attention. For long-context inference, BDLM Mamba-H reaches 19.7x the throughput of full-sequence DiffuMamba-H at 65K tokens and 3.7x the throughput of BDLM attention at 262K, showing that Mamba hybrids are a potential long-context diffusion architecture.

items.title: Researchers find 12 to 31% of weights in sparse transformers are interpretable with automated descriptions across full training distributions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Individual Parameters in Weight-Sparse Transformers Appear Interpretable
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an automated pipeline using large language models to generate and verify human-readable descriptions of when individual weights in transformer models are important for predictions. Their study found that between 12% and 31% of weights in sparse transformers can be interpreted with a single, generalizable description, a higher fraction than in dense transformers. This approach assesses the global role of weights across the full training distribution rather than focusing on specific behaviors or sub-distributions.

The method involves ablating weights and observing changes in model predictions to determine when a weight matters, then generating descriptions that are validated on held-out data to ensure reliability. The findings suggest that a significant portion of weights in sparse transformer models have identifiable functions, advancing the goal of mechanistic interpretability in neural networks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.02964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A central goal of mechanistic interpretability is to understand how neural networks work and what each individual component does. Dominant circuit-finding approaches focus on a specific behavior and reverse-engineer the role of components on the associated sub-distribution. However, past work has shown that components can have different functions that are active on different subsets of the input distribution. In this work we ask whether a single weight can be understood globally across the full training distribution by characterizing when it matters (the inputs on which ablating it changes the model's predictions). We introduce an automated LLM pipeline that writes a short, human-readable description of when a weight matters and verifies it on held-out text, crediting a weight only if its description generalizes. Across two sparse and two dense transformers, the fraction of weights that are interpretable (in this sense) is higher in sparse transformers than in dense ones, a gap that widens once unreliable descriptions are discarded. Our results show that a meaningful fraction of a sparse transformer model's weights can be interpreted: 12 to 31% of weights have a single short description that identifies what the weight is used for.

items.title: Researchers propose IsoLoCo, a model merging-inspired aggregation method that improves DiLoCo distributed training efficiency and performance in language model pre-training across varying worker counts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Model Merging Improve Aggregation in DiLoCo?
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced IsoLoCo, a novel aggregation method inspired by model merging techniques, to enhance the efficiency and performance of DiLoCo in distributed language model pre-training. IsoLoCo adapts the Iso-C merging method by incorporating Nesterov momentum, enabling it to outperform traditional DiLoCo approaches, especially as the number of local workers increases. This approach addresses the performance degradation seen in communication-efficient distributed training methods when scaling up the number of local models or training steps between communications.

The study draws a connection between pseudo-gradient aggregation in local SGD/DiLoCo and task arithmetic-based model merging, evaluating several state-of-the-art merging methods and identifying Iso-C as particularly effective. Empirical results demonstrate that IsoLoCo consistently surpasses both simple pseudo-gradient averaging and momentum-based DiLoCo across various model sizes and inner step counts, confirming that merging-inspired aggregation is a promising strategy for reducing communication costs while maintaining training quality in distributed settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03011v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model merging techniques, which aggregate independently finetuned models into one to combine their capabilities, have become a topic of significant interest in recent years, with a broad array of methods having been proposed to tackle this problem. Simultaneously, an emerging trend in distributed learning has been the use of methods such as local SGD and DiLoCo, which greatly reduce communication costs by periodically aggregating the independently trained local models. However, these communication-efficient methods have been shown to degrade in performance relative to the FLOP-matched data-parallel gold standard as the number of independent local models grows and as the number of local training steps before global communication is increased. In this work, we draw an explicit analogy between the pseudo-gradient aggregation step in local SGD/DiLoCo and task arithmetic-based model merging, establishing a straightforward way to utilize merging methods in the context of distributed optimization. We then evaluate multiple state-of-the-art model merging methods in this setting and identify one method in particular, Iso-C, as a promising approach for improving DiLoCo. We find that DiLoCo SGD with Iso-C aggregation outperforms not only simple pseudo-gradient averaging but even the momentum-based DiLoCo, despite lacking a momentum mechanism itself. Building on this finding, we propose IsoLoCo, which adapts Iso-C for distributed training by equipping it with Nesterov momentum. Our empirical evaluations on language model pre-training across varying numbers of local workers show that IsoLoCo significantly outperforms DiLoCo, with the gap between them widening as the number of workers increases. This advantage remains present across model sizes and inner step counts, confirming that merging-inspired aggregation is an effective strategy for low-communication distributed training.

items.title: Researchers introduce Transition Information Density and Positional Identity to capture structured intermediate states in neural training, demonstrating effects across phonetic and semantic mediums in a four-condition experiment [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Transition Information Density: Morphological Trajectories, Synesthetic Perception, and Structured Interpolation in Neural Training (or: The Synesthetic AI)
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the concepts of Transition Information Density (TID) and Positional Identity to capture and analyze the structured intermediate states that occur between distinct training endpoints in machine learning. These constructs were tested across multiple empirical contexts, including grapheme-color synesthesia and a four-condition experiment involving different representational mediums. The study found that probes trained on structured interpolation at defined Positional Identities showed significantly lower intrinsic dimensionality in phonetic and semantic mediums compared to controls, while visual and cross-modal mediums did not exhibit this effect.

The research employed a boundary-contour morphing algorithm called the Synesthesia Grid to instantiate TID in visual morphological space and used a nine-metric shape characterization framework alongside a four-condition experimental design. The findings indicate that the structure of Positional Identity, rather than sample count, drives the observed effects, with representational richness scaling resolution. Additionally, analysis revealed globally collapsed representations in visual space and consistent representations in phonetic space, highlighting modality-specific differences in how intermediate states are encoded.

This work provides a formal definition of TID and Positional Identity and isolates trajectory structure, data volume, and Positional Identity as distinct factors influencing neural training. The results contribute to a deeper understanding of the information content present in intermediate states during training, which may inform future approaches to machine learning model development and representation learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard machine learning training presents data as discrete endpoint pairs, omitting the structure of the space between them. This paper introduces Transition Information Density (TID) -- the information content recoverable from structured intermediate states between categorically distinct training endpoints -- and Positional Identity, the defined location of an intermediate state on the A-to-B continuum. Both constructs are grounded in three empirical contexts: grapheme-color synesthesia, the Synesthesia Grid (a boundary-contour morphing algorithm instantiating TID in visual morphological space), and a four-condition training experiment across four representational mediums. Probes trained on structured interpolation at defined Positional Identities (C3) exhibit substantially lower intrinsic dimensionality than volume-matched controls (C2) in Phonetic/Linguistic (C3: 3.33 vs. C2: 10.81) and Semantic Description (C3: 4.59 vs. C2: 8.67) mediums. Visual and cross-modal mediums do not show this effect, establishing a modality boundary condition. A fixed-N=50 comparison confirms that Positional Identity structure, not sample count, drives the effect. Resolution N scales monotonically with representational richness. Pooled TwoNN analysis reveals globally collapsed representations in visual space (0.075) and globally consistent representations in phonetic space (0.977). The paper contributes a formal definition of TID and Positional Identity, a nine-metric shape characterization framework, and a four-condition experimental design isolating trajectory structure, data volume, and Positional Identity as distinct factors.

items.title: Researchers propose Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward to align large language models with selective prediction metrics, improving risk-coverage trade-off in decision-critical AI tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligning Language Models with Selective Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced a new method called Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward (RLSR) to improve the reliability of large language models (LLMs) in high-stakes decision-making tasks. This approach focuses on selective prediction, enabling LLMs to make predictions only when confident, thereby balancing the trade-off between risk and coverage and allowing uncertain cases to be handled by humans. RLSR aligns LLMs with selective prediction performance metrics, specifically targeting the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC), to enhance decision accuracy post-training.

The proposed framework outperforms existing alignment methods that primarily emphasize correctness or calibration by achieving a better risk-coverage balance across both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks. This advancement supports more reliable human-AI collaboration by reducing errors in critical applications where LLMs are deployed.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03528v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as critical decision-making components in high-stakes real-world AI systems, rendering LLM reliability a foremost practical concern. In this paper, we focus on enhancing LLM reliability through selective prediction (SP), a strategy that allows an LLM to only predict for inputs where it is likely to be correct (i.e., coverage) and hence reduce the error rate (i.e., risk) on that portion of inputs -- flagging the remaining inputs for future human discretion. In other words, SP improves LLM reliability by balancing the risk-coverage trade-off and enabling seamless human-AI collaboration. To integrate SP into LLMs, we focus on the LLM post-training alignment stage and propose to align LLMs with SP performance metrics, in contrast with existing LLM alignment methods that focus primarily on correctness or calibration metrics. Specifically, we propose a novel alignment framework, Reinforcement Learning for Selection Reward (RLSR), which targets the area under the risk-coverage curve (AURC) -- a popular SP performance metric -- as its alignment objective. RLSR achieves substantially better risk-coverage trade-off compared to multiple alignment baselines on both in-domain and out-of-domain tasks.

items.title: Researchers show classification-head fine-tuning of Tiny Language Models under 3B parameters outperforms label generation and matches GPT-3 and GPT-4 on multiple-choice benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Punching Above Their Weight: Classification-Head Fine-Tuning of Tiny Language Models (TLMs) for Verifiable Multiple-Choice Tasks
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that fine-tuning Tiny Language Models (TLMs) with fewer than 3 billion parameters using a discriminative classification head outperforms label generation methods and achieves performance comparable to larger models like GPT-3 and GPT-4 on multiple-choice benchmarks. Their study evaluated three LoRA-based fine-tuning approaches across Qwen3 models ranging from 0.6B to 8B parameters on five benchmarks, including HellaSwag, WinoGrande, and PIQA.

The classification-head fine-tuning method showed consistent improvements of 2-3% over label generation at smaller scales (0.6B and 1.7B parameters). Notably, the fine-tuned TLMs matched or exceeded zero- and few-shot results from much larger models such as GPT-3 (175B) and PaLM (540B), setting new state-of-the-art results for the smaller Qwen3 models on several benchmarks. This suggests that efficient fine-tuning techniques can enable compact models to perform competitively on complex language tasks while running on consumer-grade hardware.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03801v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We define Tiny Language Models (TLMs) as models below roughly 3B parameters that fit on mainstream consumer devices. We study how to adapt them for and use them on verifiable multiple-choice tasks. We compare three LoRA-based fine-tuning paradigms (label generation, gold only, and our discriminative classification head) on a unified setup across several Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 8B and five benchmarks: HellaSwag, WinoGrande, PIQA, SciQ and ARC-C. Classification-head fine-tuning reliably outperforms label generation (+2-3%) at the 0.6B and 1.7B scales. items.title: Researchers introduce SALT benchmark for evaluating fine-grained uncertainty in long-form LLM generation using deterministic ground truth across six tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Evaluating LLM Uncertainty in Long-Form Generation Using Deterministic Ground Truth
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced SALT (Single-answer Atomic Long-form Target), a new benchmark designed to evaluate fine-grained uncertainty in long-form outputs generated by large language models (LLMs). SALT consists of six procedurally generated tasks with deterministic ground truths, allowing precise assessment of correctness, calibration, and confidence ranking at the unit level without relying on external judges. This approach addresses challenges in uncertainty estimation that arise from label imperfections in existing benchmarks.

Using SALT, the researchers analyzed over 50 LLMs and identified which confidence functions best capture different aspects of uncertainty. They found that confidence ranking tends to fail at the most granular (atomic) level, even when it performs better at coarser levels. The benchmark also enabled controlled experiments revealing two main sources of future errors: error propagation from corrupted prefixes and degradation linked to increasing answer-context length. Additionally, the study showed that reasoning techniques like Chain-of-Thought prompting improve accuracy but can reduce the reliability of confidence rankings.

These findings have important implications for applications where reliable error detection and mitigation are critical, highlighting the trade-offs involved in enhancing model reasoning while maintaining trustworthy uncertainty estimates.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.03870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As LLMs generate increasingly long outputs, effective uncertainty estimation must identify errors at fine-grained levels rather than discard entire responses. While such methods exist, evaluating uncertainty at any resolution (token to an entire generation) is challenging and highly sensitive to label imperfections, making zero-noise benchmarks essential; yet, long-form generation benchmarks tend to rely on fallible labels rather than deterministic ground truth. We introduce Single-answer Atomic Long-form Target (SALT), a benchmark of six procedurally generated tasks with single deterministic long textual ground truths, enabling unit-level evaluation of correctness, calibration, and ranking without external judges. Equipped with SALT, our analysis of 50+ LLMs reveals key insights: We identify which confidence functions dominate each uncertainty aspect and show that confidence ranking largely breaks at atomic resolution, even when clearer separability emerges at coarser line-level units. SALT further enables controlled atom-level interventions throughout generation, revealing two separable drivers of future errors: propagation from corrupted prefixes, dominated by global context correctness, and bounded degradation from increasing answer-context length. Finally, we demonstrate that reasoning, via Chain-of-Thought prompting or internalized through training, introduces a trade-off, improving accuracy while degrading confidence ranking. These findings directly impact risk-critical applications requiring reliable error identification and mitigation.

items.title: Researchers present ShishuRaksha AI, a training-free multimodal explainable AI framework for screening abuse-related trauma in Bangladeshi children, evaluated on noise-aware synthetic data with 0.874 AUC [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Explainable AI for Screening Abuse-Related Trauma in Bangladeshi Children: A Training-Free Multimodal Framework Evaluated on Noise-Aware Synthetic Data
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ShishuRaksha AI, a training-free multimodal explainable AI framework designed to screen for abuse-related psychological trauma in Bangladeshi children. The system integrates four screening methods—validated questionnaires, Bengali narrative text, House-Tree-Person drawing features, and facial affect—using a clinically weighted fusion approach with cross-modal attention. It generates bilingual reports with risk explanations and referral guidance to national child-protection services, addressing the lack of culturally adapted screening tools in Bangladesh.

Due to ethical constraints on collecting clinical data from abused children, the researchers evaluated ShishuRaksha AI on a noise-aware synthetic dataset comprising 500 cases with deliberate noise layers and literature-based priors. The model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.874, outperforming a baseline questionnaire-only model. The study openly discusses limitations such as reliance on synthetic data and subgroup disparities, positioning this work as a feasibility study and a step toward ethical child-protection screening in low-resource settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04010v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bangladesh has an estimated 1.17 mental-health professionals per 100,000 population and only six child psychiatrists nationwide. No Bengali-language, culturally adapted tool exists for early screening of abuse-related psychological trauma in children. We present ShishuRaksha AI, a decision-support (not diagnostic) framework that fuses four screening modalities: validated questionnaires (SDQ, CPSS), Bengali narrative text, House-Tree-Person (HTP) drawing features, and facial affect. The fusion is training-free and clinically weighted, uses cross-modal attention, and includes a single-modality override rule. Every risk score is explained through clinically weighted, perturbation-based additive attribution and rendered as a bilingual (Bangla/English) report with referral routing to national child-protection services (OCC, DSS, NMHH) under the Children Act 2013. No clinical dataset of abused children can be collected ethically at this stage, so we introduce a noise-aware synthetic benchmark (500 cases, 116 positive [23.2%], four deliberate noise layers, literature-grounded HTP priors) and evaluate tree-ensemble surrogates of the fusion design (facial channel excluded) under 5-fold stratified cross-validation. The fused model reaches an AUC of 0.874 [0.834-0.908], against 0.756 [0.705-0.803] for an SDQ-only baseline, with ablation, operating-point, subgroup, and calibration analyses. We state all limitations openly, including synthetic-only data, no held-out set, text-feature circularity, and an urban-rural subgroup gap. This work is a feasibility study and a design contribution toward ethically deployable child-protection screening in low-resource settings.

items.title: Researchers propose DynaVieW, a schema-guided world model for hierarchical visual dynamics prediction and simulation, improving visual narrative creation and world simulation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: DynaVieW: Schema-Guided World Modeling for Understanding Hierarchical Visual Dynamics
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced DynaVieW, a dynamic schema-guided world model designed to improve the prediction and simulation of hierarchical visual dynamics in videos and multi-image sequences. This model addresses the challenge of capturing multiple levels of dynamic elements, such as actions and environmental changes, by learning interleaved state-transition sequences that represent broad visual scenes and detailed dynamic constituents within a hierarchical framework. DynaVieW employs a mixture-of-experts architecture with selective attention and a specialized loss function to enhance learning effectiveness and robustness.

By jointly modeling transition prediction and state simulation, DynaVieW achieves a deeper understanding of visual dynamics, which enhances its performance in tasks like visual narrative creation and world simulation. The model demonstrates improved consistency, controllability, and adherence to instructions, marking a significant advancement in the systematic modeling of temporal visual scene evolution.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04112v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal LLMs struggle to systematically model the temporal evolution of visual scenes in videos or multi-image sequences. Such inputs require models to predict or simulate multiple levels of dynamic constituents, such as actions taken in the visual sequence, and the associated changes to the visual environment that result. To address this challenge, we propose a dynamic schema-guided world model, DynaVieW, optimized for visual dynamic prediction and simulation. DynaVieW achieves an in-depth understanding of visual dynamics by learning interleaved state-transition sequences, where states cover broad visual scenes from video keyframes, and transitions capture comprehensive dynamic constituents within a hierarchical schema. DynaVieW jointly models transition prediction and state simulation under a mixture-of-experts architecture, with a cross-expert selective attention and a schema token re-weighted loss, to ensure effective and robust learning. DynaVieW's understanding of visual dynamics boosts its downstream performance in visual narrative creation and world simulation, showing improved consistency, controllability, and instruction-following.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate practical trigger-word data poisoning attacks on smolVLA vision language action model, causing robot denial of service with minimal poisoned samples in open-source robotics [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: !Imperio, smolVLA: The Implications of Data Poisoning on Open Source Robotics
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that trigger-word data poisoning attacks on the smolVLA vision language action model are practical and effective in disabling robots with minimal poisoned samples. By introducing just a few poisoned episodes into the training data, they were able to embed a backdoor that causes a robot to enter a fixed joint configuration and fail to complete tasks on command, resulting in a complete denial of service. This attack was tested on a real-world pick-and-place task using the LeRobot platform, showing that even a single poisoned episode significantly reduces task success rates while remaining stealthy under normal operation.

The study found that the attack works across different trigger placements and poison ratios, with clean-prompt performance remaining stable, indicating the backdoor remains hidden during regular use. These findings highlight the vulnerability of open-source robotics ecosystems, which often rely on community-contributed datasets, and emphasize the need to treat dataset provenance as a critical security concern to prevent such low-cost, stealthy attacks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04146v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This work establishes that trigger-word data poisoning of vision language action models is practical, while at the same time the open-source robotics ecosystem holds trust assumptions about community contributions. A few poisoned samples can silently embed a backdoor that disables a robot on command. We evaluate this threat against smolVLA on a real-world pick-and-place task, training on three poison ratios and evaluating across different prompts on the LeRobot platform. Three poisoned episodes in 320 clean episodes suffice for a complete denial of service. Success rate drops to 0.0 plus minus 0.0% across all trigger-word conditions and the robot locks into a fixed joint configuration rather than executing any task-relevant motion. Clean-prompt behaviour holds at approx. 50% success rate across all poison ratios, confirming the attack is stealthy under normal operation. A single poisoned episode already reduces success rate to 6.7 plus minus 6.7%. The robot still moves, but no longer completes the task. The attack generalises to front, middle, and end trigger placements despite training exclusively on front-placed triggers. These findings establish that the threat is practical, low-cost, and stealthy, and warrant treating dataset provenance as a first-class concern in open-source robotics ecosystems.

items.title: Researchers present HiFA4, a training-free 4-bit FlashAttention design for LLM inference on Ascend HIF4 NPUs, improving accuracy and reducing latency across five large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: HiFA4: Training-Free 4-bit FlashAttention on Ascend HIF4 NPUs for LLM Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced HiFA4, a novel post-training design for 4-bit FlashAttention tailored for large language model (LLM) inference on Ascend HIF4 NPUs. HiFA4 executes key attention operations as 4-bit GEMMs while maintaining softmax computations in FP16, aiming to improve accuracy and reduce latency without additional training. This approach is the first of its kind evaluated on standard NLP benchmarks for Ascend-HIF4 hardware.

HiFA4 incorporates two key mechanisms: Smooth-QK, which rescales query and key matrices to ease quantization challenges, and P-Reordering, which accumulates the softmax normalizer directly from quantized attention weights, enabling fusion into the PV GEMM and reducing output-scaling errors. Evaluations across five LLMs show that HiFA4 significantly reduces quantization-induced accuracy loss and decision drift, recovering a substantial portion of the accuracy gap compared to direct quantization methods. Preliminary analysis also suggests a potential 35.4% reduction in critical-path latency by fusing operations, though on-hardware validation remains future work.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04302v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present HiFA4, a post-training operator-level design that executes both QK^T and PV in FlashAttention as 4-bit HIF4 Cube GEMMs for LLM inference on Ascend NPUs, while maintaining the online softmax state in FP16. To our knowledge, HiFA4 is the first Ascend-HIF4-targeted design of this kind evaluated on standard NLP benchmarks. HiFA4 combines two mechanisms. Smooth-QK applies a calibration-static per-channel equivalent rescaling to Q and K after RoPE, transferring quantization difficulty from K to Q without per-tile online reduction at inference. P-Reordering accumulates the softmax normalizer from the same quantized attention weights P_hat used in the PV GEMM, rather than from a higher-precision reconstruction. We show that this inconsistent formulation introduces a coherent output-scaling error, and validate the effect on a Qwen3-8B Layer-0 MMLU trace, where all 3.6M measured attention tiles exhibit net probability-mass loss with median epsilon_bar = -0.064. P-Reordering also allows the normalizer to be fused into the PV Cube GEMM. Across five LLMs, HiFA4 reduces quantization-induced decision drift. On Qwen3-8B, it recovers 37.5% of the accuracy gap introduced by direct HIF4 quantization, narrows the sample-weighted accuracy loss from 1.12 pp to 0.70 pp, reduces BF16-inconsistent MMLU predictions from 16.3% to 8.2%, and cuts MMLU accuracy regressions by 57% (1071 to 465). On Gemma2-9B, mild smoothing keeps HiFA4 within 0.7 pp of BF16 while reducing MMLU regressions by 27%. On LLaMA3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, and Phi-4B, where Smooth-QK is disabled, P-Reordering with the adopted Q-Mean auxiliary still reduces full-set MMLU regressions by 41-52%. A preliminary instruction-scheduling analysis projects a 35.4% critical-path latency reduction relative to BF16 by fusing the softmax normalizer into the PV Cube GEMM; on-hardware validation is left to future work.

HiFA4 executes key attention operations as 4-bit GEMMs while maintaining softmax computations in FP16, aiming to improve accuracy and reduce latency without additional training. This approach is the first of its kind evaluated on standard NLP benchmarks for Ascend-HIF4 hardware.

HiFA4 incorporates two key mechanisms: Smooth-QK, which rescales query and key matrices to ease quantization challenges, and P-Reordering, which accumulates the softmax normalizer directly from quantized attention weights, enabling fusion into the PV GEMM and reducing output-scaling errors. Evaluations across five LLMs show that HiFA4 significantly reduces quantization-induced accuracy loss and decision drift, recovering a substantial portion of the accuracy gap compared to direct quantization methods. Preliminary analysis also suggests a potential 35.4% reduction in critical-path latency by fusing operations, though on-hardware validation remains future work.

items.title: Researchers introduce URSA, a chemistry-aware benchmark for evaluating retrosynthesis planning methods, finding large language models underperform specialized models in drug discovery tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: URSA: Chemistry-Aware Benchmark for Utilitarian Retrosynthesis Assessment
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment), a new chemistry-aware benchmarking framework designed to evaluate retrosynthesis planning methods in drug discovery. URSA assesses synthetic routes not only by their formal criteria, such as convergence to commercially available starting materials, but also by chemical plausibility, reflecting expert chemists' evaluation approaches. The study compares specialized deep-learning retrosynthesis models and general-purpose large language models (LLMs) on novel target molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, representing realistic drug design challenges.

The evaluation reveals that while LLMs can assist with high-level strategic planning in synthesis, they currently underperform compared to specialized retrosynthesis models in reliably solving synthesis planning tasks. This highlights the need for continued development of domain-specific models to improve the accuracy and practicality of retrosynthesis predictions in drug discovery.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04688v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Synthesis planning aiming to find pathways of reactions for a target molecule is one of the most important and challenging tasks in drug discovery. Recent progress has produced both specialized deep-learning retrosynthesis systems and general-purpose large language models, but objective comparison remains difficult due to the lack of flexible, chemically interpretable benchmarking protocols. In the current study, we are introducing the URSA (Utilitarian RetroSynthesis Assessment) evaluation framework that provides the opportunity to benchmark the synthetic routes not only from a formal perspective, such as convergence to commercially available starting materials, but also from a chemical plausibility perspective, mimicking the way expert chemists evaluate the reactions and routes. The study covers a comprehensive evaluation of both conventional end-to-end retrosynthesis solutions and LLMs for the synthesis planning task on a set of novel, diverse target molecules with undisclosed synthetic routes, which represent realistic tasks in the daily drug design routine. We find that while LLMs can support high-level strategic planning, they currently underperform specialized retrosynthesis models in reliably solving synthesis planning tasks.

items.title: Researchers propose Replayed-Prefix On-Policy Distillation (ReOPD) to speed up multi-turn LLM agent training by reusing teacher trajectories, achieving 4x faster training with maintained accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation with Prefix Replay
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Replayed-Prefix On-Policy Distillation (ReOPD), a method designed to accelerate the training of multi-turn large language model (LLM) agents by reusing pre-collected teacher trajectories. This approach allows the student model to act at selected steps while receiving dense supervision from the teacher without requiring new environment interactions, resulting in training speeds at least four times faster than traditional on-policy distillation (OPD) methods while maintaining or improving accuracy.

ReOPD addresses challenges in multi-turn OPD, such as the "prefix trap," where querying the teacher on student-relevant but unreliable histories causes distribution shifts. By implementing a step-decaying sampling schedule that emphasizes early, more reliable prefixes, ReOPD effectively balances student occupancy and teacher reliability. Experiments across tasks involving mathematical reasoning and search environments demonstrate that ReOPD eliminates the need for tool calls during student training and transforms costly agent-environment interactions into reusable offline resources, enabling scalable distillation across various tools, tasks, and environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.04763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study on-policy distillation (OPD) for agentic tasks, where an LLM agent interacts with an environment over multiple turns and a student imitates a teacher over these multi-turn interaction histories. Fully online OPD is costly because each update requires fresh student rollouts through the environment and teacher queries at visited histories. We propose Replayed-Prefix On-Policy Distillation (ReOPD), an off-environment alternative that reuses pre-collected teacher trajectories as replayed prefixes: the student acts at selected steps, while the teacher provides dense per-step supervision without executing new environment interactions. We show that multi-turn OPD introduces a prefix trap: making histories more student-on-policy improves relevance to the student, but can query the teacher on histories where its target is unreliable. This creates a two-sided distribution shift between student occupancy and teacher reliability. ReOPD addresses this by treating multi-turn OPD as a reliability-aware prefix distribution design and implements it with a simple step-decaying sampling schedule that emphasizes early, lower-shift prefixes. Across mathematical reasoning with Python and search environments over multiple teacher and student model scales, ReOPD preserves or improves OPD-level accuracy, uses zero tool calls during student training, and is at least 4$\times$ faster per training step than OPD. ReOPD therefore turns expensive agent-environment interaction into a reusable offline resource, enabling scalable distillation across tools, tasks, and environments.

items.title: Researchers introduce Localized LoRA-MoE, a block-wise low-rank expert framework with adaptive routing for scalable, parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large language and perception models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Localized LoRA-MoE: Block-wise Low-Rank Experts With Adaptive Routing
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Localized LoRA-MoE, a novel framework that enhances parameter-efficient fine-tuning for large language models and high-dimensional perception networks. This approach combines localized spatial blocking with adaptive, context-driven routing to overcome limitations of existing methods like LoRA, which suffer from optimization issues due to static architectures. The framework introduces two architectures: Block-Wise LoRA-MoE with centralized routing and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE with decentralized, autonomous gating at the matrix cell level.

Extensive testing across various benchmarks, including matrix simulations, tabular data transformations, and vision tasks under sensor degradation, shows that both architectures effectively resolve optimization deadlocks found in static models. Notably, the decentralized cell-level gating matches the performance of a global coordinator, providing a robust mechanism to prevent gradient corruption. These results demonstrate that Localized LoRA-MoE offers a scalable, parameter-efficient solution for dynamic adaptation in complex and changing operational environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05114v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) and high-dimensional perception networks increasingly rely on parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) to adapt to diverse operational contexts. However, standard methods like LoRA are structurally limited by a monolithic bottleneck, making them highly susceptible to gradient warfare. Interleaved multi-task streams may trigger destructive optimization feedback, collapsing adapter weights into unspecialized averages. While recent spatial partitioning methods have introduced block-wise isolation, they remain trapped in static topologies, unable to adapt to dynamic task-switching or environmental sensor failure. In this work, we introduce Localized LoRA-MoE, a unified framework that fuses localized spatial blocking with dynamic, context-conditioned routing. We propose and evaluate two novel architectural paradigms: Block-Wise LoRA-MoE (Centralized Macro-Routing), which modulates the entire structural grid via a monolithic context signal, and Cell-Wise LoRA-MoE (Decentralized Micro-Routing), which empowers every coordinate cell in the matrix grid with autonomous, localized expert gating. Through a comprehensive suite of benchmarks, ranging from high-dimensional SVD matrix simulations and real-world tabular transformations to spatial vision perception under sensor degradation, we demonstrate that both architectures resolve optimization deadlocks inherent in static baselines. Our empirical results establish that decentralized cell-level gating achieves complete statistical parity with an omniscient global coordinator, providing a robust "gradient firewall" that protects surviving pathways from fault-propagated corruption. Our proposals consistently outperform static baselines, offering a scalable and parameter-efficient solution for dynamic model adaptation across granular coordinate fields and shifting operational regimes.

items.title: Researchers introduce noisy channel decomposition of Minimum Bayes Risk decoding to incorporate bidirectional effects and improve text generation evaluation metrics [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Noisy-Channel Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a noisy channel decomposition of Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding to address asymmetries in text generation evaluation metrics like BLEU and COMET. This approach incorporates bidirectional effects by breaking down MBR decoding into four components: hypothesis-to-reference likelihood, reference-to-hypothesis likelihood, hypothesis prior, and reference prior. This decomposition offers a unified view of existing MBR methods and enhances interpretability by isolating each channel's contribution.

The study's analysis shows that these channel contributions vary across different metrics but remain consistent across tasks, suggesting that adjusting channel weights could improve upon traditional MBR decoding. This advancement aims to produce more robust and higher-quality text generation by better aligning hypothesis selection with the characteristics of common evaluation metrics.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05198v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) decoding yields more robust and higher-quality text generation than maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding by selecting hypotheses that maximize expected utility over sampled pseudo-references. However, there exists a discrepancy in the design: hypothesis selection calculates expected utility scores conditioned on given pseudo-references, while commonly used evaluation metrics, e.g., BLEU and COMET, are asymmetric. Therefore, it is important to consider both hypothesis-to-reference and reference-to-hypothesis directional effects. In this study, we introduce a noisy channel decomposition of MBR decoding that naturally incorporates bidirectional effects to account for these asymmetries. We decompose MBR decoding into four interacting components: hypothesis-to-reference likelihood, reference-to-hypothesis likelihood, hypothesis prior, and reference prior. This decomposition provides a unified interpretation of existing MBR variants and enables metric- and task-specific interpretability by isolating the contribution of each channel. Our comprehensive analysis reveals that channel-wise contributions exhibit distinct characteristics across metrics while remaining consistent across tasks, and suggests that appropriate channel weighting may lead to improvements over original MBR decoding.

items.title: Researchers propose HeRo, a selective disclosure watermarking framework for large language models enabling fine-grained metadata access control with high detection accuracy and low latency [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Selective Disclosure Watermarking for Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed HeRo, a new watermarking framework for large language models that enables selective disclosure of embedded metadata. Unlike existing multi-bit watermarking methods that require revealing the entire embedded message for verification, HeRo allows different verifiers to access only specific portions of the watermark based on their access level. This approach enhances privacy by preventing unnecessary information exposure while maintaining high detection accuracy and low latency.

HeRo works by recursively partitioning the vocabulary and distributing watermark information across hierarchical layers, preserving the unbiased nature of the text generation process and ensuring text quality. Experiments demonstrate that this method supports fine-grained access control without compromising the underlying sampling process. The researchers have made the code publicly available for further exploration and use.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05353v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Watermarking methods embed imperceptible and verifiable signals into text generated by large language models (LLMs). Existing approaches include zero-bit schemes for distinguishing synthetic text from human writing and multi-bit schemes for embedding metadata. However, current multi-bit watermarking methods do not allow selective disclosure: verifying any part of the watermark requires revealing the entire embedded message. This lack of control leads to unnecessary information exposure and raises privacy concerns. We propose Hierarchical Vocabulary Routing (HeRo), a watermarking framework that enables selective disclosure of embedded metadata. The method recursively partitions the vocabulary and distributes watermark information across hierarchical layers, so that different verifiers can decode only the portions of the payload corresponding to their access level. We show that the proposed scheme preserves the unbiasedness of the underlying sampling process and thus maintains text quality. Experiments demonstrate that our framework supports fine-grained access control while achieving high detection accuracy and low latency. Code is available at https://github.com/xuyangc03/hero-watermark.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05369v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: For robots to work reliably in commercial and industrial applications, can recent advances in agentic coding systems combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model-free policies? We focus on "Variational Automation" (VA), a class of tasks that have larger variations in object geometry and pose than fixed automation. Model-free policies often struggle to close the reliability gap for VA tasks, which must be executed persistently and reliably in commercial and industrial applications. Motivated by prior work on Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) and the Robot Operating System (ROS), we introduce Graph-as-Policy (GaP), a multi-agent coding harness that generates directed computation graphs with perception, planning, and control nodes from a Modular Open Robot Skill Library (MORSL). GaP then generates an internal simulation environment to rehearse task instances with different graphs in parallel to iteratively refine the graph structure and parameters to improve success rates and throughput. Evaluation with 8 new open VA task benchmarks, 4 in-simulation and 4 in real-world, suggests that GaP can achieve success rates that significantly outperform baselines. Details, code, and data can be found online: https://graph-robots.github.io/gap

items.title: Researchers derive continuous-time Markov chain ELBO for discrete diffusion models, proving the Oracle Distance theorem and identifying optimizer coordinates across denoiser, score, and bridge plug-in predictors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What Does a Discrete Diffusion Model Learn?
items.summary:
Researchers have derived a continuous-time Markov chain evidence lower bound (ELBO) for discrete diffusion models, establishing the Oracle Distance theorem which states that the negative ELBO equals the data entropy plus the path KL divergence from the oracle reverse process to the learned one. This result identifies the unique optimizer as the conditional expectation of the true reverse jump rate given the current noisy state, showing that all noising processes share the same optimal negative ELBO equal to the data entropy.

The study further reveals that for sequences with token-factorizing noise, the optimizer can be expressed in three exact coordinates—denoiser, cavity (bridge plug-in), and score—with closed-form conversions among them. This framework clarifies which loss functions in existing literature correspond to which optimization laws, explains differences between masked and uniform diffusion, and addresses issues such as ELBO divergence at initialization under certain parameterizations. All theoretical identities were numerically verified on an exactly solvable model without approximation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05381v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What does a discrete diffusion model learn: a denoiser, a score ratio, or a bridge plug-in predictor? At the level of jump rates, these are one object in different coordinates, and reading a neural network in the wrong coordinate changes the process being trained and sampled. Starting with a rigorous derivation of the continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) ELBO for any noising process, boundary terms included, we prove the \emph{Oracle Distance} theorem: the negative ELBO is exactly equal to the data entropy plus the path KL from the oracle reverse process to the learned one, not merely a bound. Its unique optimizer is therefore the conditional expectation of the true reverse jump rate given the current noisy state, and its irreducible cost is the rate at which the forward process $Z_t$ destroys information about the clean data $Z_0$, $-\tfrac{d}{dt}I(Z_0; Z_t)$, so every noising process shares the same best achievable negative ELBO: the data entropy. For sequences with token-factorizing noise, the oracle projection yields three exact coordinates for the optimizer: denoiser, cavity (bridge plug-in), and score, with closed-form conversions among them. This framework identifies which law each loss in the literature actually optimizes, recovering MDM, UDM, SEDD, and GIDD as special cases; explains why denoiser and cavity coincide for masked diffusion but not for uniform diffusion; proves that a denoiser parameterization makes the uniform ELBO diverge at initialization while the bridge plug-in stays finite; and calibrates ELBO implementations exactly at initialization. Every identity is verified numerically, without approximation, on an exactly solvable model.

items.title: Researchers introduce LLM-as-a-Verifier, a general-purpose framework providing fine-grained verification and continuous scoring for agentic tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM-as-a-Verifier: A General-Purpose Verification Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have developed LLM-as-a-Verifier, a versatile verification framework that enhances the ability of large language models (LLMs) to assess the correctness of solutions in agentic tasks. This framework generates continuous scores by computing expectations over scoring token logits, allowing for fine-grained feedback without additional training. It improves verification accuracy by scaling score granularity, repeated evaluation, and criteria decomposition, and achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks including Terminal-Bench V2, SWE-Bench Verified, RoboRewardBench, and MedAgentBench.

The approach introduces a cost-efficient ranking algorithm to select the best candidate solutions based on continuous scores and provides detailed signals that can estimate task progress. An extension for Claude Code has been developed to help developers monitor and enhance their agentic systems. Additionally, LLM-as-a-Verifier offers dense feedback for reinforcement learning, boosting sample efficiency in robotics and mathematical reasoning tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2607.05391v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scaling pre-training, post-training, and test-time compute have become the central paradigms for improving the capabilities of LLMs. In this work, we identify verification, the ability to determine the correctness of a solution, as a new scaling axis. To unlock this and demonstrate its effectiveness, we introduce LLM-as-a-Verifier, a general-purpose verification framework that provides fine-grained feedback for agentic tasks without requiring additional training. Unlike standard LM judges that prompt LLMs to produce discrete scores for candidate solutions, LLM-as-a-Verifier computes the expectation over the distribution of scoring token logits to generate continuous scores. This probabilistic formulation enables verification to scale along multiple dimensions: (1) score granularity, (2) repeated evaluation, and (3) criteria decomposition. In particular, we show that scaling the scoring granularity leads to better separation between positive and negative solutions, resulting in more calibrated comparisons. Moreover, scaling repeated evaluation and criteria decomposition consistently lead to additional gains in verification accuracy through variance and complexity reduction. We further introduce a cost-efficient ranking algorithm for selecting the best solution among candidates using the verifier's continuous scores. LLM-as-a-Verifier achieves state-of-the-art performance on Terminal-Bench V2 (86.5%), SWE-Bench Verified (78.2%), RoboRewardBench (87.4%), and MedAgentBench (73.3%). Beyond verification, the fine-grained signals from LLM-as-a-Verifier can also serve as a proxy for estimating task progress. We build an extension for Claude Code, enabling developers to monitor and improve their own agentic systems. Finally, we show that LLM-as-a-Verifier can provide dense feedback for RL, improving the sample efficiency of SAC and GRPO on robotics and mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers propose Direct On-Policy Distillation to transfer reinforcement learning policy shifts from smaller to stronger models, boosting Qwen3-1.7B performance on AIME 2024 by 14 percentage points in 4 hours [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Direct On-Policy Distillation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD), a method to transfer reinforcement learning (RL) policy improvements from smaller, less costly models to stronger, more complex ones. This approach addresses the challenge of expensive RL training on large models by leveraging the policy shifts learned by smaller models and applying them as implicit rewards to enhance the performance of larger models without retraining from scratch. Using Direct-OPD, the team significantly improved the Qwen3-1.7B model's performance on the AIME 2024 benchmark, increasing accuracy from 48.3% to 62.4% within four hours on eight A100 GPUs.

Direct-OPD works by comparing a smaller model's policy before and after RL training, using the difference as a dense reward signal for the larger model's own on-policy states. This technique bypasses the need for explicit reward models or sparse-reward RL on the target model, enabling efficient reuse of RL supervision across model scales. The method outperforms traditional direct RL approaches and supports sequential application of multiple policy shifts, demonstrating a scalable way to generalize RL improvements from weak to strong models.
